en: The Attainment of Freedom from Action (Naiṣkarmyasiddhi).
Now begins the first chapter.
Since all living beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, naturally desire to abandon every form of suffering, there is an activity directed toward its cessation that arises quite spontaneously.
Because suffering has the appropriation of a body as its sole cause, and because the body is rooted in dharma and adharma accumulated in the past, there is no cessation [of suffering].
Because those two (dharma and adharma) are rooted in actions that are enjoined or prohibited, there is no termination [of them].

Because action has passion and aversion as its basis, and because passion and aversion are bound to the superimposition of "the beautiful" and "the ugly," and because superimposition is caused by the non-investigated reality of duality, and because all duality—like shell-silver and the like—is based solely on the non-apprehension of the self which is inherently established as non-dual, there is no removal [of duality].

Therefore, the non-comprehension of the Self alone is the cause of all evils. Since bliss—which is free from coming and going and independent of anything else—is the very nature of the Self, its non-comprehension constitutes a veil. Consequently, when that [veil] is completely eradicated, there is the full accomplishment of the ultimate human goal. And because the cessation of ignorance has as its sole cause the attainment of the nature of right knowledge, that [right knowledge] must be acquired. Furthermore, since the object of the non-comprehension of the Self—the cause of all evils—is not within the scope of worldly means of knowledge such as scripture-based inference or perception, right knowledge arises only from the sentences of the Vedāntic scriptures.
Therefore, this treatise, which is a compendium of the essence of all the Vedāntas, is now commenced.
In this regard, the following is the first verse, intended both to set forth the multitude of desired topics and to provide a summary of the meaning of the entire work:
From whom [proceeds] that which extends to ether, air, fire, water, and earth, rising up like a garland upon the hood of a serpent...
Salutations to that Hari, the witness of the intellect, who cuts through the darkness. || 1 ||

In order to make known that his own tradition is preceded by the means of valid cognition as enjoined, [the author] performs an act of salutation to the Guru, preceded by a proclamation of the connection with his distinguished qualities:
"Salutations to that most venerable one, who severs the knot of ignorance, from whom darkness and the other [afflictions] have turned away because they have not attained any excellence. (2)
This is for the purpose of manifesting my own intention through salutation:

"I shall explain, by the instruction of my Guru, that knowledge which is hidden within the womb of the Vedānta, which transcends saṃsāra and pertains to the ultimate reality, even though it has been expounded by others. (1.3)

If it is asked what is the subject matter of this treatise, the following is presented: That upon whose establishment the "I" (the ego) is established, and upon whose non-establishment nothing at all is established—the true nature of that which is solely grounded in the attribute of inwardness shall be clearly explained. (4)

In order to inspire confidence in the subject matter of the intended treatise, and by dispelling doubts regarding the lack of authority in what has been left unsaid or poorly said, the author describes the authority of his own teacher:
"The established doctrine of the Vedas was taught by my teacher; I do not speak of it here due to my own incapacity.
What could a firefly illuminate when the sun with its thousand rays pervades the sky? (5)

If it is argued that since the meaning of the Vedas has already been fully established by the Guru himself, there might be a suspicion regarding the lack of authority in this treatise due to motives such as fame, [the author] says the following to dispel that: "This work is not uttered by us for the sake of fame, profit, or honor;
rather, it is for the purpose of purifying our own understanding, like testing-stones for those who know Brahman. (6)

This introduction is offered to make known the summary of the subject matter: the undesirable, the cause of the undesirable, human goals, and their causes. That non-realization of the identity [of the self] which relies upon the appearance of one's own self as [something else] is ignorance;
it is the seed of transmigratory existence. The destruction of that [ignorance] is the liberation of the self. (7)
Because the purpose of human life remains unfulfilled, there is the expression of that [purpose].
The fire of right knowledge arising from the final words of the Vedas utterly consumes one's own delusion, for action is not opposed to it.
The statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the thesis.
In that regard, first making an assumption regarding knowledge, it is introduced as follows:
"Since liberation is accomplished by means of ritual actions, what does knowledge do in that regard?"
And how it was—listen to all of that with a focused mind.
For one who does not perform actions for the sake of desire, who likewise abandons prohibited acts, and who duly performs the obligatory and occasional rites; || 10 ||

What follows from this? Consequently, the fruit of optional (kāmya) actions does not approach him from that god or other deities; and because prohibited actions have been cast aside, he does not undergo a lower birth in hell.
Regarding the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) that initiate the body, the objection and its resolution are the same for both the knower (*jñānin*) and the agent of action (*kārmin*).
By whichever two—merit and demerit—this present body, which bestows pleasure and pain, was begun, their exhaustion occurs only through experience (*bhoga*). (12)

If it be argued that since transmigratory existence is the fruit of optional and prohibited actions, and since the removal of all evils is accomplished by the mere elimination of those [actions], what is the use of performing obligatory duties (*nityakarman*), we say: no. For from the non-performance of them, evil would still result; and through the performance of obligatory duties, demerit (*pratyavāya*) shall not touch him.
Therefore, disregarding the knowledge of the Self, one should take recourse to ritual actions. (13)

This is stated merely as a concession; however, there exists no knowledge whose object is the self as it truly is, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that.
For as many Śrutis as exist here, together with the Smṛtis, they prescribe with great effort rituals that require abundant means. (14)

If it is argued that there might be the possibility of a means of valid cognition [for the existence of God] due to some error on our part, we say no; because: "Even though I examine with great effort, I do not see anywhere a scriptural injunction for [the existence of] knowledge [of God], whether in the Śruti or the Smṛti; nor do we have any basis for trust other than these. (15)

If it be argued that activity may occur even without an injunction, as is seen in the world, we say no; for: "Whatever one might perform for the sake of the hereafter out of delusion, without an injunction, that would not be of benefit, like an oblation poured into ashes. (16)
Furthermore, because of the teaching of Jaimini, who knows the meaning of the Veda and whose authority has been accepted:

"Since the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has action as its purpose, anything other than that is purposeless"—thus did Jaimini, the knower of the Veda himself, proclaim loudly and with great emphasis. (17)
And because of the wording of the mantra:
"Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years.
This mantra also enjoins the performance of action throughout the entirety of one's life.

Furthermore, since the wise accept the authority of a sentence regarding an existing entity (*vastu*), and since a sentence has the verb as its primary element, there is consequently an absence of the intended knowledge [of that entity].
Indeed, words do not coalesce at all without an action;
there is no sentence consisting of non-words that could be a prescriber of knowledge. (19)

Even if knowledge is accepted [as a prerequisite], there is no fault; because, in this context, the relationship [between action and knowledge] is established either through the relation of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) or by virtue of its own predominance (*svapradhānatā*), and thus, even when knowledge exists, there is no defect. (20)
Since liberation does not result from knowledge alone, whether such knowledge is accepted or rejected,
therefore, for all stages of life, liberation shall come through the performance of actions of speech, mind, and body according to one's capacity, and not by any other means. (21)
Anticipating the objection that "this is mere prattle regarding a non-existent object," he says:
"Thus, indeed, the words of those with delighted minds—whose hearts are puffed up with their own wisdom—are proclaimed in the sacrificial halls by those whose intellects are obscured by smoke. (22)
To make known the beginning and limit of the refutation, he says:
"In this matter, we shall state the faults one by one with words strengthened by logic, which strike down the statements of the prima facie position, and not out of excessive haste. (23)
Since none of the four types of results of action are possible in liberation, liberation is not the result of action.
Because liberation consists merely in the destruction of ignorance, action is not its means.
Action wipes away [impurity], but it does not remove ignorance, just as light cannot dispel the darkness arisen within darkness. (24)
Even if one accepts that liberation is the result of karma, there is still a fault:
would liberation come from a single action, or from all actions?
If it were from each individually, then the others would be useless; if it were from all together, then they would constitute a single action. (25)

Since every kind of action is connected from its very inception with a specific result to be accomplished, the logic of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) cannot be established [for the purpose of proving that obligatory rites lead to liberation].
Because they serve the purpose of exhausting past sins, obligatory rites (*nitya*) would not lead to liberation;
likewise, because they are connected to results such as heaven, optional rites (*kāmya*) do not lead to it either. (26)
And because no means of valid cognition is possible [for such a claim]:
"This relationship between the goal and its means is based on the word [of scripture] regarding the world beyond;
I have never heard from the mouth of a Vedic teacher that ritual action bestows liberation. (27)
Furthermore, because you have accepted what has already been accepted, your idle chatter is as pointless as the words of a mother-in-law who has just left the house.
You yourself desire the abandonment of both prohibited and optional acts just as I do;
and since the obligatory rites bear no fruit, liberation cannot be accomplished by ritual action.

Thus, this position—that liberation is accomplished through ritual actions—has been refuted. Now, by examining the cause for the engagement in all ritual actions, the author, desiring to strengthen the position that the cessation of all the evils of saṃsāra results solely from the pure knowledge whose object is the reality of the self as it truly exists, says:

In this regard, the following is examined: Is it the case that, just as with prohibited and arbitrary actions, one—on account of the influence of innate tendencies and the motivations arising from one's own disposition—imagines distinctions such as "this is beneficial" and "this is harmful," and then, like one thirsty for the water of a mirage, proceeds and desists by oneself to attain the beneficial and avoid the harmful by employing only those means established by worldly authority; or is it otherwise in the case of rites performed for unseen purposes, whether optional (kāmya) or obligatory (nitya)?

In this regard, [it is said] that "the cause for engagement and withdrawal" [is the means of knowledge]. What follows from this? Listen: if it is determined that correct knowledge of an object as it actually exists—whether worldly or scriptural—is the cause for engagement, and the scripture concerning withdrawal is not accepted, then those who renounce ritual action are ruined; for they rely solely on erroneous cognition and abandon the performance of rituals acquired through non-worldly means of knowledge.

If, like the causal basis for the activity of one thirsty for the water of a mirage, it is merely a mistaken consciousness (*bhrānti-vijñāna*) regarding what is not actually real that serves as the cause for all activity, then we are the victors and you are the defeated!

"For those who, out of delusion, desire to obtain what is beneficial and wish to avoid what is harmful, the scripture illuminates the means for attaining and abandoning [these ends], like the sun. (29)

Thus, first of all, by relying on the means of valid cognition—perception, inference, and scripture—it is established that the Self is inseparable from unsurpassed happiness and welfare; and since that which is harmful is, like the sixth object [non-existence], inherently unconnected to it, it follows that the failure to realize this very nature of the Self gives rise to the false cognition, "May there be welfare for me" and "May there be no harm for me. This false cognition, like the false cognition arising from the non-realization of mother-of-pearl as silver, is determined to be the cause of worldly activity. Furthermore, it has been established that scripture does not create the power of things.
Now, a detailed elaboration of this very point is commenced hereafter.

For a treatise does not create in a person either the desire to acquire or the desire to abandon; for those two [impulses] belong only to one's own nature, since they are seen even in animals and the like.

It has thus been stated that it is only one who has not yet realized the true nature of things who is eligible for the treatises on injunctions and prohibitions: "Out of ignorance, one desires what has not been obtained, like a golden necklace around one's own neck;
and one avoids what is already one's own by delusion, like mistaking one's own shadow for another. (31)
With his mind shrouded by fear and delusion, the Rākṣasa seeks to avoid what he has already abandoned and desires to obtain what he has not yet acquired. (32)
In this regard, the method for attaining and avoiding these four objects is demonstrated by way of analysis:
"Having learned the means separately from the sacred tradition regarding what is to be attained and what is to be avoided, one should then act;
thus one may attain what is to be attained and likewise abandon what is undesirable. (33)

Now, as for the two remaining [obstacles], they are abandoned by their very nature. Since the attainment of what has not yet been attained is through realization, abandonment and attainment do not occur through karma.
Because these two have only delusion as their obstacle, they are not accomplished by ritual action. (34)

Why, then, do the attainment of the desired, unsurpassed happiness and the cessation of all suffering arise from the mere realization of the true nature of the self-substance, and not from ritual action? It is said in reply:
Because action originates from ignorance, it is not capable of removing delusion;
right knowledge is its opposite, just as the sun is to darkness. (35)

[Objection: But surely even the knowledge of the Self has ignorance as its material cause (*upādāna*), for the knowledge of the Self does not come into being without depending upon the scriptures, the disciple, the teacher, and so forth. [Reply: This is not a fault. Because the knowledge of the Self, by the mere fact of resting upon the true nature of the supreme reality of the Self which is established by itself, destroys ignorance along with the entire collection of causal factors produced by it; thus, it requires the scriptures only for its own origination, not for the cessation of ignorance once it has arisen. Action, on the other hand, [requires them] both for its own origination and once it has arisen.

For an action does not sustain itself for the sake of yielding a fruit that is separated by tens of millions of eons while being devoid of any desire for an agent, because its nature consists solely in the fact that it is being accomplished. Nor does an action connect the agent with a fruit such as heaven at the very moment of its own attainment, like the knowledge of the Self. On the other hand, the knowledge of the Self requires no other form or other means beyond its own nature as it arises for the accomplishment of the human goal. Why is this so? Because:
"Right knowledge arising from a powerful means of valid cognition is never sublated."
Nor does it seek any other means for the sake of sublation. || 36 ||
Since one's own position has been established by the support of logical reasons, it is concluded without hesitation:
"Therefore, for the removal of ignorance—the cause of the ocean of suffering—right knowledge is entirely sufficient; action is not [required], because of the reasons already stated. (37)

Objection: But surely we observe that even powerful right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is sublated by that which arises from what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), since even for one who has produced the awakening to ultimate reality (*paramārtha-bodha*), cognitions arising from the non-comprehension of agency, enjoyership, passion, aversion, and so forth, continue to manifest. For when right knowledge is unsublated, there can be no possibility of cognitions contrary to it. Reply: This is not so. Why?
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) has been sublated, it cannot sublate knowledge (*vidyā*).
Rather, its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) certainly become the cause for the recollection of knowledge. (38)

The reason stated as "because it arises from ignorance regarding karma" has already been supported by the passage beginning with "those desiring to attain the beneficial. To further strengthen that point, I shall demonstrate how [the self] is subject to the cycle of transmigration through its connection with ignorance; therefore, he says:
"Having conceived the notion that 'I am not the Self' regarding the body which consists of Brahminhood and so forth, one becomes a servant to the Veda in the actions of speech, mind, and body. (39)
Since karma arises solely from ignorance, it is said that when that [ignorance] is removed, [karma] ceases.
If a sage has burnt away all his remaining obligations by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman, he, standing at the pinnacle of the Veda’s teaching, would no longer be a servant of the Vedas. (40)

Then, the other person—whose inner organ is enveloped by a dense veil of ignorance, who has accepted all causes for the entitlement to action such as agency and so forth, and who is gripped by the pair of injunctions and prohibitions—engages in actions.
Through auspicious deeds he attains the state of a deity; through prohibited deeds, the state of a denizen of hell;
and through both merit and demerit, he helplessly obtains human birth. (41)

From the peak of Brahma down to a blade of grass, within this terrible ocean of suffering, one is driven like a water-wheel by the mechanism of ascending and descending. Impelled by the winds of mixed good and evil karma, one is cast into various wombs—fickle as flashes of lightning, yielding pleasure, pain, and delusion according to whether they are inferior, middling, or superior. Like a dried gourd tossed in the midst of the ocean, battered by the force of the fierce and turbulent winds, thus does this being wander, bound by ignorance, desire, and action;
possessed by craving, he is born and dies, enveloped in misery. (42)
To instill reverence for the meaning as it has been stated, an authoritative source is presented:

Scripture has declared this matter for the sake of the cessation of desire, because worldly existence (saṃsṛti) is rooted in that [desire], and its destruction results from the removal of ignorance. (43)
If it is asked, "What is that scriptural passage? [the answer is:
"When all are completely liberated," and "Thus indeed," according to the Vājasaneyins.
Vyāsa also has stated at every step that this is merely the bondage of desire. (44)

This path of saṃsāra has been explained. Now, for the sake of turning away from it, it is described how ritual actions (karmāṇi) become causes for liberation by way of providing remote assistance (ārādupakārakatva).

For one who is thus tormented by suffering, through some practice of merit (puṇyaśīlanāt), detachment (vairāgya) arises in the heart of one whose intellect has been purified here by the obligatory rites (nitya). (45)
What kind of dispassion arises? It is said:
Just as he previously felt fear toward hell, so too does he feel it toward the fruits of desire;
thus, through the vision of reality, he desires to perform obligatory duty (nitya-karma) forevermore. || 46 ||

Thus, as that mind is being purified by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites through actions dedicated to the Lord, it becomes perfectly stainless and then manifests dispassion toward the world of Brahmā and other realms. (47)

Because the mind, being thoroughly tainted by the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, is dragged away by the hook of desire and cast into the slaughterhouses of sense-objects which lead to endless suffering; therefore, by the cleansing of the performance of obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), the mirror of the mind remains with its stains of *rajas* and *tamas* cast off, serene, unshakable, resembling a polished crystal slab, and no longer dragged by the hook of the "seizers" (*atigraha*) consisting of passion and hatred caused by external objects—it stands with all defilements shaken off, inclining solely toward the Inner Self. Hence, this is stated: [The verse follows: *Yasmād rajastamomalopasaṃsṛṣṭameva cittaṃ kāmabaḍiśenākṛṣya viṣayadurantasūnāsthāneṣu nikṣipyate, tasmān nityanaimittikakarmānuṣṭhānaparimārjanenāpaviddharajastamomalaṃ prasannamanākulaṃ saṃmārjitasphaṭikaśilākalpaṃ bāhyaviṣayahetukena ca rāgadveṣātmakenātigrahabaḍiśenānākṛṣyamāṇaṃ vidhūtāśeṣakalmaṣaṃ pratyagmātrapravaṇaṃ cittadarpaṇam avatiṣṭhate.* *ata idam abhidhīyate:* [The verse follows. (Note: The provided text ends with the introductory prose for the verse, so the translation reflects that structure.)
When the mind, having emerged from all desires, remains steady,
it then enters of its own accord into the innermost Self.
From this point forward, those actions whose authority has come to an end—having been entrusted to a son who is inclined toward the inner self—are fulfilled.
Having produced in the intellect an inclination toward the inner self through purification, actions, having achieved their purpose, set like clouds at the end of the rainy season. (49)
Since this is the greatness of the performance of obligatory rites,
therefore those seeking liberation who desire self-knowledge must always perform obligatory and occasional rites for the sake of the constant purification of the self. (50)

Regarding the matter stated above, the word of the Omniscient One is the authoritative source. Furthermore, the Smṛti states: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility alone [is the means]. (Gītā 6.3) || 51 ||

From the performance of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) arises merit (*dharma*); from the arising of merit comes the destruction of sin; from that, purification of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*); from that, the realization of the true nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-yāthātmyāvabodha*); from that, dispassion (*vairāgya*); from that, the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*); from that, the search for the means thereto; from that, the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of all actions and their instruments; from that, the practice of yoga (*yogābhyāsa*); from that, the inward orientation of the mind (*pratyak-pravaṇatā*); from that, the thorough comprehension of the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*); from that, the eradication of ignorance (*avidyā*); and from that, abiding in one's own Self alone, as it is said: "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman" and "Being liberated, he is liberated."
In this way, action alone may lead indirectly to the cessation of ignorance;
however, unlike knowledge, action does not dispel ignorance because it is not its opposite. (52)
Not even the slightest effect of action is possible in liberation, nor does that which is possible in liberation depend upon action. This is stated:
"The fruit of action consists of that which is to be produced, attained, refined, or modified;
since liberation is none of these, action is not its means. (53)

Thus, it has been explained in detail that ritual action alone is not sufficient for the direct removal of ignorance. Furthermore, regarding liberation, it has been stated—in the passage beginning with "for those seeking the beneficial"—that every form of ritual action is impossible, in accordance with the nature of the knowledge of one desiring liberation and its object.

It has been demonstrated how the combination of ritual actions (*karma*) is possible for the arising of knowledge by way of being an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). Now, however, it is stated that regarding the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is only self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), having attained its own essential nature, which possesses the unique status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*); no other [means], whether primary or secondary, possesses it.
In this regard, he first states that knowledge is not a cause when it is secondary:
"And knowledge does not dispel the ignorance that is [the result of] action by coming into direct contact."
Because of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, they cannot exist at the same time. || 54 ||
Even the possibility of both being equally primary is non-existent;
because of the relationship of the sublated and the sublator, like that between a lion and a jackal, there can be no combination of the two, as they cannot coexist in the same place. (55)
Whence could there be the relationship of the sublated and the sublator? Because:
Ignorance would be that which does not correspond to reality, while knowledge is its opposite;
thus, their coexistence is impossible, like that of the sun and the darkness. (56)

Therefore, when there is the complete realization of the Self as Brahman—which is devoid of agency—the injunctions for all ritual actions become blunted, because their very nature becomes subject to questioning. How so? It is explained: just as a Kṣatriya does not participate in the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice.
Whether a Brahmin or one who possesses the conceit of "I" regarding being a Brahmin, [he may engage] in the duties of a Kshatriya.
He states that just as it is with this illustration, so it is with the subject of the illustration:
"Videha, whose doubts have vanished, for whom nothing remains except 'not this, not this,' likewise does not even perceive action, having seen the body and so forth as non-self. (58)
To illustrate that point, there is this example:
"Just as a child, superimposing the nature of an elephant upon a clay elephant, frolics about;
so too does the deluded person act, having superimposed the body and other such things upon the Self. (59)

Nor do we deny the relationship between knowledge and action in all cases whatsoever; where there exists the relationship of the instigator and the instigated between knowledge and action, even our father could not prevent it. To demonstrate the distinction therein, an illustration is shown:
"Just as one who mistakes a post for a thief flees in fear, so too does the deluded person act by superimposing [the self] upon the intellect and other [faculties]. (60)

Thus, wherever there exists a relationship between knowledge and action as that of the employed and the employer, this principle applies everywhere. However, where a combination is established neither simultaneously nor sequentially, it is said to have an object [of application]. Just as the true knowledge of a post does not fail to serve as a limb when one flees, so too the true knowledge of the Self does not fail to serve as a limb in the injunction of action. (61)
For this is the inherent nature of a quality (*guṇa*):

that which follows the nature of another in accordance with that other's requirements must be subordinate to it, since a quality does not exist independently of the primary substance (*pradhāna*). || 62 ||
For this reason:
Knowledge that requires the context of a ritual action becomes a quality of that action;
for whatever belongs within the context of something is declared to be its subsidiary (aṅga). (63)
That knowledge which destroys our ignorance merely by its own manifestation cannot, in any case, be either a subsidiary or a primary factor of ritual action. (64)
Even by one who maintains the position of synthesis (samuccaya), this must necessarily be admitted:
for knowledge itself cannot be established without first eliminating ignorance.
Knowledge does not approach a village where the performers have failed. 65.
And this is another reason for the refutation of the combination of knowledge and action:
Their causes, essential natures, and effects are mutually contradictory, like light and darkness; therefore, there can be no conjunction of knowledge and action. (66)

When this has been established, some, relying on the strength of their own tradition, say: "The realization 'I am Brahman' which arises from the Vedāntic statements does not dispel ignorance merely by its own birth. What then? For one who meditates day after day over a long period of time, ignorance departs entirely through the accumulation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), according to the Śruti: 'Having become a god, he goes to the gods.'"

Others, however, say: "The cognition 'I am Brahman' produced by the Vedānta statements does not indeed penetrate the true nature of the reality of the Self, because it consists of a synthesis [of concepts]. What then?

For one who practices this very same [cognition] continuously like the flow of the Ganges, another distinct cognition arises, which consists of the meaning of the sentence as a whole. To refute these two positions, this is stated: "By its single occurrence, it crushes that which bears the form of action and its factors."
Ignorance and scriptural knowledge are incompatible; therefore, there is no coexistence between these two.

Thus, the combination of knowledge and action within a non-dual Brahman has first been refuted. Now, even if one were to argue by accepting an alternative position, the lack of confidence [in that view] is explained just as before:
"Even according to the opinion of that proponent for whom Brahman does not exclude plurality, the combination of knowledge and action is difficult to establish. (68)
The statement regarding its classification is for the purpose of designating the classification of its defects:

"Whether that [object] be the Self, which is Brahman, or whether it be of the nature of the non-Self, there would be a failure to attain the Self due to delusion regarding the other, namely the non-Self. (69)

In that regard, if Brahman is already attained by its very nature through its actual mode of being, such that the sole cause for its non-attainment is merely the veil of demonic delusion—in that case, ritual actions are not at all the means for breaking the veil of delusion;
since the fruit is obtained through knowledge alone, action is useless therein. (70)

But in the case of Brahman, which is of the nature of non-self, action does not attain the status of a means, nor does knowledge—whether combined with action or uncombined—attain it; because for Brahman, who is himself the self-evident accomplisher, any state of being "other" than that is established by its very nature.
In this regard:
"When one thing attains the nature of another, no cause whatsoever is possible."
Even though that exists, it is not lost; it attains the Supreme Self. || 71 ||

But according to the other view, there is a positive injunction: even those who perceive duality, if they are suffering, may be liberated through the practice of knowledge that is favorable to the Supreme Self, but not through that which is opposed to the Supreme Self. (72)
But in the other case, there would be no room for the injunction at all. How so?
"Tell us, what cause could there be for ritual action for one who perceives the non-difference of all things from Brahman, and who abides in Brahman alone, whether as the whole or as its parts? (73)
Furthermore, through the occurrence or non-occurrence of the causes for all actions, the confusion of all actions would follow. For this reason:
If this [self] possessed all [the qualities of] birth and so forth, the production of causes would be utterly impossible;
for action does not proceed at all without taking up a specific [condition]. (74)
If it is argued that there might be a positive injunction [regarding the self] due to the conceit of the internal self (*adhyātmābhimāna*), it is not so; because:
"Even for the knower, there is no conceit of the internal self, owing to its demonic nature (*āsuratva*).
If even a knower were to possess a demonic nature, the vision of Brahman would be fruitless. (75)

Since ignorance is the effect [of knowledge], there can be no conjunction between knowledge and action—neither simultaneously nor sequentially—because they depend respectively on the real and the unreal; yet, although thus refuted, he speaks while grasping at straws like *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass.
Furthermore, if one should again proceed inwardly, he would become dependent and deluded;
he indeed performs actions, for who can restrain an ignorant man? (76)
Furthermore, because it is already established, it is not something to be accomplished. For this reason:
"For this yogin, the very nature of his action consists of both the universal and its opposite;
therefore, like inhalation and exhalation, it does not depend upon an injunction. (77)

Let it be, then, that Brahman consists of both difference and non-difference; for in that case, knowledge and action would be possible, as their respective objects are difference and non-difference. To this, we reply: this very position is not possible. Why? Because the cognition of difference does not embrace an object without first setting aside the cognition of non-difference, such as "this is different. For if this were not admitted, the categories of "different-and-non-different" would result in being something outside the realm of experience (*alaukikatva*).

Now, if even that which lacks any means of valid proof (*pramāṇa*) is resorted to, since both positions are accepted, it would follow that Brahman is suffering under the view of non-difference; therefore, he says:

"If [Brahman] were both different and non-different from the particularities (*viśeṣa*), then Brahman would certainly be a sufferer for you; moreover, there would be the state of being all suffering. Oh, what wisdom this is for those who profess the Self! (78)
Therefore, it is rightly stated that there is no combination of knowledge and action; thus it is concluded:
"Just as darkness cannot be an attribute of the sun, just as coldness cannot be an attribute of fire, and just as heat cannot belong to water, so too action cannot be an attribute of knowledge. (79)

Since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been refuted by the very force of the arguments stated above, there remains nothing further to be said; nevertheless, because something must be said to refute the prima facie position—just as one performs a rite of realization (*pratipatti-karma*)—the following is now declared:
"Because liberation is accomplished through ritual actions," and so forth, much that was stated is improper. That which was asserted is unjust; how it is so shall now be explained. (80)
This vow which is undertaken—the renunciation of both optional rites and prohibited acts—cannot, for the time being, be carried out. What is the reason?

For action, once its nature has been brought into existence, ceases in two ways: that which has begun to bear fruit ceases through experience, and that which has not yet begun to bear fruit—being unwholesome—ceases through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). There is also a third mode of cessation, namely through the realization of the Self as a non-agent; however, because you do not accept the knowledge of the Self, you do not admit this mode. Among those [actions], those whose fruits have not yet been experienced and whose fruits have not yet begun cannot be abandoned even by the Lord or by anyone else.
If it is argued that those whose fruits have begun are abandoned, even those cannot be abandoned.

What is the reason? Because [the action] has not been completed. For an action intended to be performed that is not yet completed can be abandoned, since the agent possesses independence regarding both engagement and withdrawal. But once the action is completed, that is impossible; thus, the meaning of the vow would be difficult to carry out. Furthermore, it is impossible to make such a vow. One cannot vow, "For as long as I live, I shall not perform optional or prohibited actions," because even the most skillful are seen to commit subtle transgressions. Moreover, there is a lack of authoritative evidence [for its feasibility].

Furthermore, there is no authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for the claim that "one who desires liberation should perform obligatory and occasional rites, avoid those performed for specific desires and those that are prohibited, and exhaust those whose fruits have already begun through experience. This is because they are infinite. There is no limit to the accumulated karma, since saṃsāra is beginningless. Nor can there be the cessation of those [karmas] by means of optional or prohibited acts, because when purity and impurity are equal, there is no contradiction [between them].
Thus he says: "The total renunciation of all optional acts is not intended to be accomplished because of their infinity;
as for prohibited acts, however, they were committed in infinite past births. (81)

It might be thought: "The destruction of those karmas acquired over infinite past births occurs through obligatory rites (*nitya*), just as sin is destroyed by expiations (*prāyaścitta*); however, because they are fruitless, obligatory rites do not bring about the cessation of optional (*kāmya*) and other such acts. (82)

And because there is a lack of authoritative evidence. How so? Just as penance is understood from a scriptural statement for the removal of sin, so too is occasional (kāmya) action understood [from scripture] for the purpose of abandoning desire; but obligatory (nitya) action is not [understood] from a scriptural statement in that way. (83)

Now, it might be argued that the exhaustion of those [karmas] accumulated in previous births which are to be experienced as desirable results will occur precisely through [the performance of] rites for desired ends (*kāmya*). That is not so; because:

"Just as there is no removal here of evils by means of other evils, let it be the same with desirable results: [there can be no removal] of desirable results by means of [other] desirable results, due to their lack of opposition. (84)
Thus, for now, the argument that "liberation is established through ritual actions" has been refuted.
Now, having stated that there is no proof for the existence of knowledge of the Self, he says the following to refute that objection:
"Because they are infinite, the Śrutis, together with the Smṛtis, prescribe here for those possessed of desire, with great effort, rituals that grant many desires. (85)
Furthermore, multiplicity does not constitute a cause for validity. Therefore, he says:

Multiplicity is not [the cause] for validity; for valid means of cognition do not converge upon a single object. Rather, when there is a single object, there is validity for only one [cognition]. (86)
As for what was said—"even though looking with great effort"—in that case too, the fault is yours alone. Why? Because:
"Do you not hear those excellent Vedic texts, such as 'having examined the worlds,' which enjoin the knowledge of the Self and lead toward the state of actionlessness? (87)

[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of scriptural injunctions such as "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone" and "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," a mandate for the person regarding the act of seeing the Self is determined? [Response: It is not so;
for the knowledge of the true nature of reality—which dispels the non-comprehension of the Self, the seed of all misfortune, and is the cause of liberation—is not dependent on the person.
Even if an injunction were admitted, this is not an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction). Therefore, he says:

Since the meaning of the injunction may also be a restrictive rule (niyama) or an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), we worship the Supreme Self solely through the non-perception of the non-Self. (88)

As for what was said—"We have no trust in anything else"—that too was merely the ravings of you, whose mind is afflicted by sleep and who are dreaming. What is the reason? It is because we do not establish the identity of the Self (*aikātmya*) through the force of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since that identity consists solely of self-evident experience (*anubhava*). For this very reason, he will later state that it is impossible for any means of valid cognition to apply [to it].
This is because the establishment of the system of valid cognitions rests upon experience alone.
Therefore, he says:
One should not place trust in a reality that is accessible solely through verbal testimony and is not established by any other means;
but how could there be a lack of trust in the Self, which is self-evident and not an object of measurement? 89.
As for what was also stated, "without an injunction," that too appears to us as if it were not preceded by conscious reflection;
for this [objection] would apply only to those actions whose fruits are to be realized at a later time.
Regarding the knowledge of the Self, which bestows its fruit at the very moment of its own attainment, he says that this [objection] is not tenable:
"When this fruit has been obtained through knowledge—which is directly perceived and destroys rebirth—it does not appear reasonable to us to say that it does not lead to benefit. (90)

As for the statement of Jaimini that you have cited—that too is raised merely because his intended meaning has not been fully understood. What is the reason? Because this was not Jaimini’s intention: that the entire Veda is solely for the purpose of ritual action (*kriyārtha*).

For if such had been his intention, he would not have composed the venerable *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], which investigate the meaning of all Vedāntas, are woven with profound reasoning, and are devoted to revealing the true nature of the reality of Brahman through such aphorisms as "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) and "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādyasya yataḥ*). Yet, he did indeed compose it.

Therefore, this is precisely Jaimini’s intention: that just as injunctive sentences possess authority regarding their own literal meaning alone, so too do the sentences concerning the oneness of the Self, because they are equal in their determination of a previously unknown reality. Consequently, the following is stated: "If it be granted that the Veda which exists beyond [mere] injunction has only the purpose of action, then tell me: how could sentences such as 'That thou art' have the purpose of ritual action? (91)
Moreover, just as in the doctrine of a single self (aikātmya), activity toward actions whose results are unseen is difficult to perceive, so it is in your position as well. For:
"One desiring to go to heaven should offer the Agnihotra according to the rule;
how then, for Jaimini, can there be agency for one who has been separated from the body? (92)

Furthermore, there can be no entitlement to ritual action for a mere self whose nature consists solely of the instruments of action—such as the body and so forth—which have been rejected [by the opponent]. For this reason:

"How indeed could Jaimini, who does not wish to accept the object denoted by 'you' (the non-self), be impelled [to teach] one who is not possible through any means of valid cognition and whose sole instrument is the notion of 'I'? (93)
And because there is an absence of a cause for activity; for this reason:

"The connection of the Self with pleasure, pain, and so forth is not perceived by me, because [the Self] is inward-turned while [objects] are outward-turned. How then is Jaimini urged [to argue otherwise]? (94)
Furthermore:
There is no connection whatsoever between the self and the body;
since there is no contact with sense objects even at a distance, how could there be happiness in heaven and such realms? (95)
Because it would otherwise be untenable,
the Mantra— accepting the person who conceives the pride of being a human and who views the self as an agent and so forth— says "acting," and not [addressing] one who is free from duality. (96)

As for what was said regarding the phrase "setting aside," that too is not entirely correct. Nevertheless, not just any action (*kriyā*) should be supplied (*adhyāharaṇīyā*) wherever or whenever; rather, only that action which is capable of establishing the intended connection and fulfills the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the sentence should be supplied. And such a specific action has indeed been accepted by us. Moreover, that action—being consistent with the intended meaning of the sentence—is not one whose result is the manifestation of an unreal object.

Since the reality of the Self—which is devoid of the six modifications of existence, from which all the evils of duality have been washed away, and whose luminosity is independent of anything else—is what one desires to make known, one must accept that verbal forms such as "I am" (asmi) are capable of conveying an object established by their own inherent power, and not intended to convey a contrary meaning.
Just as the word "run" (dhāvet) is not employed in the sense of "giving," so too one should not desire [words like] "prosper" (edhi) and the like to express an object that is self-established. (97)

Furthermore, it cannot be determined that the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and so forth expresses any other meaning apart from the demonstration of the actual nature of the reality as described; thus he says:
"Because the sentences 'That thou art' and so forth convey a meaning established by its own nature, no other meaning can be perceived even by the gods. (98)

Since this is so, therefore, for all stages of life (āśramas), liberation cannot be attained through well-performed actions of speech, mind, and body; for that [liberation] comes from knowledge alone. 99.
For this reason, the following is also established:
Therefore, those words of those whose intellects are puffed up with a wisdom fashioned by their own desires shine only among the Vedic scholars, not among the knowers of the Self. (100)
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.

It has been demonstrated through numerous arguments that perception and the other means of knowledge do not have the Self as their object, because they are restricted to objects that constitute their own specific domains; and because the Self is distinct from all objects of knowledge (*prameya*), it is only the words "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)—which are capable of illuminating the true nature of reality—that serve as the cause for the rising of the sun of knowledge which dispels ignorance, the sole cause of all misfortune.
Therefore, this second chapter is commenced to remove the obstacles that prevent the comprehension of that meaning.

If one who has been instructed does not understand the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" because of a lack of familiarity with the referent of the term *tvam*, then for that reason the method of its analysis is stated.

I have previously stated that this meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman," or the realization thereof, arises from the sentence alone, because perception and other means of knowledge do not have such a thing as their object; now, for the sake of clarifying that point, its lack of uniformity is presented as a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa):
"Upon the cessation of the entire non-Self, one attains peace;
another [attains it] through the recollection of the heard sentence; and yet another is reminded by the spoken word. (2)
In this context, he mentions another alternative for the sake of providing a possibility in both cases:
"And by merely hearing the sentence, one may obtain [the result] like a Piśāca;
in three cases success is accidental, but when it is being reminded, it is certain. (3)
This reason is not inconclusive; for:
"All this greatness should be known as belonging to the sentence alone, as previously stated;
indeed, no one knows the meaning of a sentence in its true essence apart from the sentence itself. (4)
And a sentence, having been set forth for the purpose of conveying a meaning, certainly conveys it, because all means of valid cognition function in this same manner.

For one who understands this sentence, "Thou art That," no contradiction arises regarding the self as being graspable, nor as being dependent on that [body], nor as being the inner witness, nor as being the sufferer. (5)
For one who is not dispassionate toward saṃsāra, there can be no desire for liberation from it; nor can a person whose thirst has not ceased possess the longing for liberation.
And for one who does not desire liberation, there is no approaching the feet of a guru here;
nor can there be hearing of the sentence without a connection with a guru.
Likewise, words and word-meanings do not exist anywhere without a sentence; and without those two, upon what could positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) depend? (8)
Without positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), there can be no comprehension of the meaning of a sentence;
and without that, the abandonment of ignorance is not possible.
Without the abandonment of ignorance, the goal of human existence is very difficult to attain;
therefore, the subsequent text is introduced for the sake of accomplishing what has been stated. (10)
Just as feces is not understood to be the self because it is a product of food, why is the body—which is a portion of that [feces] and possesses the senses—not likewise regarded as such? (11)
Since it is well-established that [the body] is non-self at the beginning and at the end, what obstacle is there to its being so in the middle as well?

That which was previously non-self, having been consumed, attains the state of self through ignorance—like a garland or an ointment applied to the body; therefore, one of discerning intellect should view the body as distinct [from the self]. 12.

If you do not heed my words even in this way, you will yourself become hopeless regarding this body, which is but a heap of impurities. You think "I am" only so long as you have not been led away from it; once the body has been devoured by dogs, you will no longer conceive such an identification.
Having stepped upon the head with his foot, he scorns other dogs;
seeing that the body is common to all, why, O friend, are you so attached to it? (14)
This point—that everything from the intellect down to the body is non-self—is established by scripture; thus he says:
"Just as a single seed is divided into three parts consisting of chaff, grain, and husk, so too food exists [in the body] in three parts consisting of intellect, flesh, and excrement. (15)
When the aforementioned meaning has been understood, the wise person is not perturbed by passion or hatred; to demonstrate this point, there is the following illustration:
"When excrement has been completely discarded and determined to be a foul thing, if someone were to speak of its foulness, what effect would that have on the one who uttered it? (16)
In the same way, when both the subtle and the gross bodies have been abandoned through discernment, what fault could there be for the wise man regarding those two? || 17 ||

Indeed, this alone is the cause for not realizing the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman": namely, the unbroken and firm grasping of "I" and "mine" with respect to everything from the intellect down to the body.
For when that [grasping] is absent, one is not divided from anything at all, but abides as the one, non-dual inner Self; thus he says:
"For one who perceives the same single identity in enemy, friend, and one's own body..."
How could there be anger in one who possesses discernment, [toward those who cause harm], as if toward the limbs of one's own body? (18)
For this reason as well, the body and so forth are not the Self:

because they are objects of perception like a jar, because they are perceived by those very same instruments [of sense] as the Seer, and because there is no continuity of them in dream; thus the wise know that the body is not the Self. (19)

For one who perceives both the distinction and non-distinction between the Self and the aggregate of the body and its instruments, a contradictory effect is perceived through direct perception itself:
"That very body which is carried by four [elephants] with all their power becomes like a tuft of cotton for those mindless ones when it is seized by the notion of 'I'. (20)
To conclude the meaning of the section by way of what is well-known, he says:
"Having thus rejected the gross [body] through reasoning, like the blueness of the sky, one should therefore reject the subtle body of the self by means of reasonings. (21)
How might one discard the subtle body? It is said:
"I-ness, mine-ness, effort, and desire are not attributes of the Self, because they are perceived as objects of action and because they are subject to loss, like a garment. (22)

This is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta): Fire does not burn its own heat because it is of the same nature as itself, just as fire [does not burn itself]; in the very same way, one should know that the Self does not burn the Self, for there is no distinction between them. 23.

Having heard that the status of being both the object and the agent of action for a single self is in no way tenable, the Mīmāṃsaka objects: "The self is the grasper because it is grasped by the notion of 'I'. To refute that, he says:
"For whatever entity is the object of a certain [cognition], it cannot have that same [cognition] as its agent;
since the cognition of a jar [is not the agent of the jar], therefore the 'I' could not have the seer as its object. (24)

Here, an objection is raised: since the agency of the self is accepted on the basis of perception, it is improper for inference—which depends upon that very perception—to set aside perception; this is the challenge. To refute it, perception is presented: "When something is seen by a seer, that quality belongs only to the object seen, and not to the seer;
for what resides in the seer cannot become an object of sight, just like the consciousness of the seer itself. (25)

Since perception as conceived by you has been shown to be a mere semblance by means of direct perception itself, inference remains well-established. Therefore, that very [inference] is set forth here, along with the statement of the refutation of the alternatives regarding it:
"A quality is not apprehended as established in its own right, neither by the self [of the substance] nor by a part thereof;
because [the substance] is non-different [from its qualities], because they are equal, because it is partless, and because there is no action. (26)
In order to demonstrate that it is not possible for a single subject (dharmin) to possess the status of both the apprehended and the apprehender—either simultaneously or successively—he says:
"Because it is already employed as the seer, at that very moment it cannot be the seen;
if its state of being the seen occurs at another time, then it is not accepted as being without a seer. (27)

[Objection: "Let it be granted that possessiveness (*mamatva*) and the like are not attributes of the Self (*anātmadharma*), since they are established as non-Self by the force of the reasoning already stated and because they are conventionally designated as such. However, as for the nature of 'I' (*aham-rūpa*), its status as a non-Self attribute is untenable; for it is well known precisely through its connection with the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), and because of the scriptural text, 'I am Brahman' (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*). [Reply: This is not so. If the attribute of "I" were non-different [from the Self], then from the statement "I am Brahman," [the following would follow]:
"The statement 'I am fair-complexioned' (*gauraḥ aham*) would be inconclusive; that statement is what removes [such a misconception]. (28)

How does that statement remove it? It is said: Just as the notion of a post is removed by the cognition "this is a man," so too the entire sense of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi) is indeed set aside by the cognition "I am Brahman. (29)

When the delimitation of the "I" (ahaṃpariccheda) is removed, not a single thing belonging to the realm of duality remains unremoved, because all connection with a second [entity] is rooted therein. Therefore, he says: "When the notion of 'I' has ceased, the cognition of 'mine' dissolves; for that [cognition of 'mine'] is established with the 'I' as its seed. In the absence of darkness, how could there be a snake? (30)
The explanation of the example is for the purpose of making known the specific portion of the example intended [to illustrate the point]:
"For one whose mind is overcome by darkness sees a snake in a rope;
because of delusion, and not without delusion, one does not perceive a snake in a garland. (31)
Furthermore, because it does not persist, the ego (ahaṅkāra) is not a property of the Self.
For if the ego were a property of the Self, it would persist during liberation and deep sleep;
since it does not persist, this "I" must belong to something else.
Furthermore, if one accepts that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is a property of the self (*ātman*), an unavoidable fault ensues:
if the ego-sense were a property of the self, it would be eternal, just like consciousness;
and if it were eternal, the treatises on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would certainly become purposeless. (33)

If it be argued that there may be a rebuttal—namely, that even if one accepts [the Self] as having an inherent nature (svābhāvikadharma), it is like the fruit of the mango and so forth—that is not so.
For the mango and such are subject to transformation (pariṇāmin), whereby there is a loss of qualities through other qualities;
but that Brahman is changeless, according to the Śruti: "For there is no seer other than the Seer. (34)

Furthermore, because the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is subject to appearance and disappearance, its substrate would necessarily follow as being impermanent. For consciousness (dṛśi), by virtue of being dependent on that which appears and disappears, would itself incur impermanence;
indeed, a property that comes and goes causes modification in its substrate. (35)
If it is argued, "Let there be impermanence; for whom shall we blame, since [this] is established by valid means of knowledge?"—that is not so.

The state of being an eternally unimpaired witness, which is self-established, cannot be denied of the Self, even by one with a mind as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, just as it cannot be denied of a jar.
For this reason as well, let it be understood that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is not of the nature of the Self:
because the "I-perceiver" is cognizable by means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), like a jar or other objects;
for how could that which is the object of the means of valid knowledge be established by those very means? (37)
Because the property and the substratum possess mutually contradictory natures, there is no connection between them.
Furthermore, because the substratum is itself contradictory [to the perceived quality], it cannot be connected with a visible quality;
coldness does not seek to enter fire whose flame is stirred by the wind. (38)
Therefore, approach with confidence:
the state of being a seer and the state of being seen can never exist in one and the same thing at one and the same time.
The seer is not the object of sight, nor is the act of seeing the seer of the seer. (39)
Furthermore, it would follow that all worldly transactional activity (*saṃvyavahāra*) would cease to exist. For:
"If the seer were also the self of the visible object, then the intellect would become an object;
simultaneity, invisibility, and the futility of scripture would result. (40)
Why? Because:
"That which has not lost its power of vision cannot be an object of sight; if it were an object of sight, how could it possess the status of a seer?
If there were only one Seer, there would be no object of sight; or else, the entire world would be without a witness. (41)
To strengthen the reasoning already stated, an example from scripture is presented:
"Everything other than the Seer is afflicted," and "Not this, not this"—how can the Śruti, which repeatedly declares Brahman to be devoid of attributes (nirguṇa), be disregarded? (42)
"The great elements and the ego—this is called the field (kṣetra).
Even according to the doctrine of Viśveśvara, there is no connection with duality for the Seer. (43)
Now follows the conclusion regarding the subject at hand:

Thus, this duality—which is to be known as manifold, falsely established, devoid of self-nature, rooted in delusion, and extremely difficult to comprehend—should be [resolved] through reasonings concerning the Self. (44)
If it is asked, "From what [source] does the falsity of duality arise?"—[the answer is:
There is no establishment of any entity other than the Self as something separate from the Self.
Therefore, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth are merely imagined within the Self, just like the Self itself. (45)
Therefore, this is merely a manifestation of ignorance:
"The objects of sight, such as sound and so forth, are established [as real], and the seer is Brahman devoid of attributes;
yet I, bearing both of these, project an illusion upon myself. (46)
Therefore, this very notion of difference regarding the non-different Self arises:
"The one Seer shines as many among all beings through the objects of sight, like the rays of the sun appear divided by the diversity of water-vessels. (47)
An illustration for the sake of understanding the meaning as stated:

Just as one and the same person is perceived as a friend, a neutral party, or an enemy based on the mental construction of others, so too, although the mind is undivided, its differentiation is based upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 48 ||
Just as the sun is reflected from all sides by water-vessels, so too is the self perceived by the intellects through the acquisition of their respective functions, forms, and locations. (49)
Furthermore, there is no impossibility of contradictory properties coexisting in a single locus;
because imagined things lack ontological reality, they can even exist in one place, just as the qualities of being desirable, impure, and sweet may coexist in a single woman. (50)
And this appearance, consisting of action, agent, and fruit, does not touch the ultimate reality even in the slightest, because it has mere delusion as its material cause.
Through attachment to what is unreal, this [world] deceives itself, just as Somaśarman’s father did when there was no second object present. (51)
With eyes veiled by the film of ignorance regarding the true nature of reality,

a man— due to the delusion of mere conceptual construction— embraces as "Rāma" that which is impure, though she possesses beautiful brows, a beautiful nose, a beautiful face, beautiful eyes, and a lovely smile. (52)

Egoism alone is the root of every class of undesirable things that one wishes to abandon, because of its attachment to the Self as being the Self. However, in the ultimate sense, there has never been, is not, nor will there ever be any connection between the Self and ignorance or its effects, because the nature of the Self is to be unstained by vision. When the seer is colored by the seen, and the seen is colored by the seer, both are colored by the function of "I-ness" (ahaṃ-vṛtti); upon the destruction of that, the non-duality of the Self remains.

Here, some raise this objection: "This 'I'-conception (ahaṃkāra), which has been discarded as non-self through positive and negative concomitance for the sake of understanding the meaning of the Great Sentence, has instead turned out to have a contrary meaning; for, since one hears the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement 'I am Brahman' (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), it follows that there is coreferentiality with something that is not the Self. Furthermore, its function regarding the inner Self must be explained. This is now stated by means of well-known figurative functions (*lakṣaṇā*, *guṇavṛtti*):
"For even one who has risen from deep sleep says, 'I did not know [anything].'"
Therefore, the characteristic of the Supreme Self is like that of the burning of iron and so forth. || 54 ||

Because it is inward-turned, extremely subtle, and because of the constant cultivation of the vision of the Self, one perceives [the Self] through the mental modification of "I," having abandoned all other modifications. || 55 ||
It would either be inseparable from the self or else undergo destruction; it could not go to any other alternative. Therefore, it is spoken of by means of the notion of "I. (56)
What, then, is the object to be characterized?
It is the Plenum (bhūman) beyond name and the rest—partless, without an agent, and without action.
That alone is the Self of those who possess the Self; it is that very thing which is established for us by its own nature.

Having first accepted the Self as being characterized by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of agency consisting of the intellect and so forth—which arise from ignorance—the fact that "I am happy" and "I am miserable" is stated through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be a property of the non-Self, such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), because it would be impossible and fruitless to maintain [agency] for the isolated Self alone.
Now, however, relying upon the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) which is imagined by ignorance, he speaks in order to negate all transformations such as agency:
"This one, whose vision is unimpaired, watches the dance of all the intellects."
Though not looking, he gazes; though blinking, his eye-brows remain fixed upon that which is impermanent.

[Objection: But surely, since all philosophical systems are established only from the perspective of their own respective views and are poorly situated from the perspective of one another’s views, we see no basis for trust in any single one; nor do we perceive any path that has been established without being refuted by any logician, which might serve as a retreat from the onslaughts of all logicians. [Reply: It is said: Let those who are confident consider this, because all the systems of logicians take recourse in experience alone.
This is stated: "Aiming at this judge (the seeker of truth), those who are severely afflicted by the fever of logic..."
They delude one another with nets of armor extending from their skin to their heads.

Regarding this, they also raise an objection: whether one accepts or does not accept that there is modification in the nature of experience itself, there is indeed a fault. For it has been said: "What effect do rain and sun have on the sky? Their effect is only upon leather.
If the self were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were equal to the sky, it would be as non-existent as nothing. (60)
If the birth of cognition in a person constitutes a modification, then it is impermanent;
on the other hand, if this cognizer is indeed unmodified, that is not tenable.
The refutation of this is as follows:

When smoke rises upward, does it pierce the sky or not? If it does not pierce it, then it must be stationary; if it does pierce it, then what kind of piercing could there be for that which is already space? (62)

To demonstrate this, he says: "The state of being an enjoyer belongs to that which is changeless due to the delusion of the notion of 'I', just as the perception of motion in stationary trees arises from the delusion of a moving boat. (63)
Another illustration is adduced to clarify the meaning as it has been stated:
"Just as the bright, blazing, and steady flame of a genuine gem undergoes no change whether jars and other objects are near or far away. (64)
To make it known that this is the point intended here, he says:
"In whatever state [the capacity] manifests, in that very state it is said again not to manifest when jars and other objects are absent. (65)
And in that regard:
likewise, the Supreme Self is the illuminator of all cognitions;
it remains changeless whether those mental modifications are present or absent. (66)
No activity of illumination whatsoever exists within its own self;
that which is the presence of illumination is metaphorically called its activity. (67)
Do not suspect that this is the final conclusion of the Sāṃkhya school; for:
"Just as a mass of clouds suddenly appears and then dissolves in the pure sky, even so does this entire world dissolve here within the Self. (68)
Therefore, this immutable [Self] does not touch even the slightest bit of duality; for:

"Through the eyes, which perceive forms that appear as sound and so forth and perish in every moment, the one, eternal Self—whose vision is non-sequential—seems to pervade the cognitions incessantly. (69)
And this being the case, it is logical that cognition is subject to transformation;
for since cognition knows all objects—past, future, and present—simultaneously, like the self, it must therefore be transformative. (70)
And from this, the following is established:

Not seeing, yet seeing the intellect that sees; likewise, not hearing, yet hearing the intellect that hears; effortless, changeless, and desireless, [the Self] beholds even the desiring intellect with its vision unimpaired. (71)

Being himself free from hatred, he should not hate one who hates him; being himself free from anger, he should not be angry with one who is angry; being himself free from suffering, he should not feel suffering for one who suffers; and being himself free from happiness, he should not feel happiness for one who is happy. (72)

Remaining undeluded, he repeatedly caused her, who was deluded, to imagine; though she was imagining, he did not imagine; and while she was remembering, he did not remember; and while she was sleeping, he remained awake.

The formless one [perceives] all forms; he whose own purpose is fulfilled perceives that which has no purpose; the motionless perceives the moving; the immutable perceives that which is momentary; and he who abides beyond the three times perceives that which exists within the three times.
Free from dependence, the non-dual inward Self beholds the dependent, outward-turned [world]— which has limits, lacks measure, and exists within all bodies.
For this reason, let this matter be determined:
if the self were suffering, who could be the witness of the sufferer? It is illogical for one who suffers to be a witness, and likewise for a witness to be a sufferer. (76)
To provide an explanation of the preceding [verse], he says: "Without undergoing modification, one cannot be a sufferer; how could there be witnesshood for that which is subject to change?
Since I am the witness of thousands of modifications of the intellect, I am therefore unchanging. (77)
Thus, in order to establish through experience that while everything else is variable, the reality of the Self alone is non-variable, he says:
"In valid cognitions and their semblances, there is no cessation of my consciousness.
Whatever form appears other than myself must indeed be subject to momentary destruction. (78)
Just as for a jar or for space, there is no arising, abiding, or destruction during [the states of] arising, abiding, and destruction; so it is for me and for the intellect as well. //79//
Furthermore, because the connection with pleasure and pain is directly perceived, this is not something to be accepted through faith alone.
Just as a spectator observes a man with a staff by means of the staff, so too does the unconditioned witness observe the intellect along with its connection to pleasure, pain, and the like. (80)
For this reason as well, it is logical that cognition is subject to modification:
because at the very moment cognition is in conjunction with pleasure, a jar, or the like, it perceives that [object] and simultaneously perceives something else; therefore, it is not immutable. (81)

And regarding its state of momentary destruction, the Self itself is the witness; for without the immutable consciousness, there can be no establishment of the appearance and disappearance of the intellect alone. The activity of the transforming intellect undergoes the sixfold modifications of existence, pervaded by the eternally non-sequential Self, just as a sprout is pervaded by the sky. (82)
The reasoning for the immutability of the existent Self is as follows:
In memory, dreaming, and waking, there is no cognition whatsoever that is not pervaded by the Seer; therefore, the Self is eternally immutable and self-luminous. (83)

Thus, by means of logical arguments, it has been established according to the system accepted by others that there is a single self devoid of all modifications. Now, however, it is stated by resorting to the scriptural system:
"Or let there be a transformation of this Seer from its immutable nature;
even so, it is merely a false construction, like the curvature of a stick in water. (84)
Since the six modifications of being have thus been denied in the Self,
no fault whatsoever can be imputed here by the dogs of logicians.
Taking up the subject at hand, the transformability of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the immutability of the Self (*ātman*) are stated through logical arguments:
"The intellects, directed toward objects, differ with respect to each object;
yet all of them are like consciousness (*cit*), since there is no difference perceived in their nature as cognition. (86)

It refers only to an object connected with itself; for this very reason, it does not know everything, as its cognition is limited and possesses a remainder [of the unknown]. Otherwise, if the intellect were to transform [into all objects], it would become omniscient, just like its own self. (87)
Therefore, because the realization is one and the same:
that which is the object of the Caṇḍāla’s perception is itself the object of the Brāhmaṇa’s perception;
that light is one for both, appearing as many only due to the difference in the objects illuminated. (88)
Why?
Because there is no difference between these two in terms of state, place, time, and so forth;
therefore, the single light perceives the activity of the cognitions of the world as being one with existence. || 89 ||

If it is argued that, since the Self is one in all bodies, even for one who has realized the supreme reality, there would still be a connection with all the sufferings associated with unawakened bodies, we say: no. Even prior to awakening, our state of suffering does not arise from another body; how then could such suffering exist after awakening, when even what belongs to one's own self is seen to be non-existent? (90)
And this should not be taken as a mere product of one's own imagination. Why?
Because it is supported by scripture (śruti).
[The scripture states: "That which has the appearance of the forms of sound and so forth, and which possesses the nature of rejection and acquisition..."
The Śruti declares that the vision of the unchanging Self is "it speaks. (91)
What is that scriptural passage? "One cannot see the Seer, the Self, by means of that which is seen;
O, by what could one know the Knower, the Lord of thoughts? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
Since this reality is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those who speak otherwise than this are to be pitied like those born blind; thus he says:

"This very non-dual Brahman, which is changeless, is conceptualized in millions of ways by those of dull intellect, just as [the elephant] was perceived by the blind men in the analogy of the elephant. (93)
The compassion for such a person is established because they find it impossible to believe in a matter that is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is what [the author] says:
"Whatever qualification is observed does not belong to oneself, because of the lack of connection thereto."
Therefore, like an empty jar or similar object, the self must be devoid of qualifiers. || 94 ||
Therefore, because difference is by nature false, the Self is untouched by difference; thus he says:
"Since this universe, together with the ego, comes and goes like a jar upon the realization of the Self, it must therefore be like [the appearance of] hair [in the sky]. (95)
The fruit of the entire operation of inference is precisely this: the apprehension of discrimination.
This is stated:
that the intellect (*buddhi*) is not a property of the Self (*anātma-dharmatva*) is established through inference.
The non-duality of the Self is established by the very fact of its being the Self. || 96 ||

Although this transmigratory world—extending from Brahma down to a blade of grass—consisting of the grasper, the grasping, the graspable, the act of grasping, and its fruit, has been discarded like a withered flower as being non-self through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, it does not depend upon the categories of the non-self or primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as something distinct from the self-established Self, as the Sāṃkhyas maintain.
What then?

It depends solely upon the non-comprehension of the Self, which is established without inquiry and reflected within the body of the self-established, unarisen, and undecaying consciousness of the Self alone; for that [non-comprehension] is its material cause. Desiring to explain this point, he says:
"Objects do not exist apart from cognition; yet cognition exists even without them.
Thus, having distinguished the light [of consciousness] as separate from the intellect, one should understand this through inference. (97)
