Since the conventional operation of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has as its very basis the non-comprehension of the Self, it is therefore established that the Self is not an object of knowledge. For an effect never establishes itself elsewhere than in its own cause, bypassing that cause to find a locus in something that is not its agent.
Therefore, he says:
"These things—the intellect, the body, the jar, and so forth—are indeed separated [from the Self]."
Since the self is of the nature of the self, by what could there be even the slightest obstruction? (98)

Because it does not possess the nature of self-apprehension, and because it lacks apprehension due to having only delusion as its material cause, these [factors] such as cognition are unestablished in the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Since the Self desires the fruit of experience, why would it require anything else? 99.
This is a restatement of the aforementioned distinction for the purpose of establishing the mutual superimposition (adhyāsa) that is about to be described:
"Just as the cognition of a jar is distinct from the jar, its object, and the seer, so too the cognition of 'I' is distinct from the 'I'-object, the sufferer, and the Seer. (100)

Thus, he states that for these two—the self and the non-self—which are established neither by themselves nor by another, their mutual superimposition is based solely on ignorance (avidyā), just like the worldly superimposition of a snake upon a rope: "Just as one, through delusion, falsely perceives a flight of clouds in the moon, so too does one imagine the attributes of the intellect, such as happiness and the like, to belong to the Self. (101)
Just as a person of deluded intellect conceives of fire as having the quality of burning iron, so too, through delusion, one attributes consciousness to the agent [of action]. (102)

This entire distinction between self and non-self, falling within the domain of means of knowledge such as perception, exists only within the embrace of ignorance (*avidyā*) and does not depend upon the Supreme Self. If it is asked, "From what source does the cessation of this ignorance—the cause of all misfortune—arise?", he says:

"This long-standing delusion is the root of this manifold mass of suffering and of the tree of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); its sublation occurs through the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*). (103)
If it is asked, "How is it possible that its sublation occurs through the vision of reality? it is said in response: This very fact is well known even to cowherds, shepherds, and scholars alike:
knowledge arising from valid cognition sublates knowledge arising from invalid cognition;
likewise, the sublation of the notion of the self in the body and so forth is like [the sublation of] the snake in a rope. (104)
Because the Self is distinct from worldly objects of knowledge, the result of valid cognition here is not the apprehension of what was previously unapprehended;
rather, the result is metaphorically described as the mere destruction of ignorance.
It is not logical that [the result] consists in making known the unknown, because [the Self] has the single nature of pure realization. (105)
Since the knower and the other categories have as their sole material cause the non-recognition of the Self, therefore:

Those who are the objects of the seer and the seeing do not know the existence of the Self, nor do they know one another; hence, for these [categories], the state of being an object of knowledge has distinct means of accomplishment.
To make known the unique nature of the seer and so forth, he says: The external object possesses form and is the grasped; the instrument of grasping consists of ascertainment and the like;
that which persists as "I" is to be known as the cognizer; but the Self is the witness, eternally constant. (107)

The Self is void of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which consists of the differentiation between agents, actions, and fruits; this is stated because the Self is the witness to that very differentiation of agents, actions, and fruits:
"He who is undivided amidst the division of the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable;
who is the witness of rejection and acquisition, yet himself devoid of rejection and acquisition. (108)
If it is asked why the distinction between the existence and non-existence of the subject and so forth is not established as residing within the subject itself, he says:
"Having perished by itself, it does not know its own destruction because of its absence;
for this very reason, it does not [know] others either; therefore, this [distinction] has a distinct witness. (109)

If it is argued that because the existence of the subject and so forth is established by a witness other than themselves, and the self-witnessing subject likewise requires another witness, this leads to an infinite regress—this is not so, because the witness does not depend on any cause external to itself. Therefore, he says: "Like the intellect, the Self does not require establishment from anything else, for It is changeless;
others, however, are established only by depending upon that which is independent, but not by themselves. (110)

Since the sense of selfhood regarding the subject and so forth is rooted solely in ignorance, therefore, having distinguished the non-self by yourself through positive and negative concomitance— know that "I am" that which remains as the unchanging witness of the world throughout its arising, persistence, and destruction, and not that which is perishable.

Because the non-self—the illusory net of duality—is established only through mutual dependence on the nature of one another, arising from the ignorance of the Self whose existence is unexamined and reflected in the self-established consciousness of the Self;
and because it is not established by itself, non-duality is established through the sublation of duality, neither by the non-self itself nor by the conscious Self, nor by both together. (112)
The citation of scriptural passages is presented for the sake of strengthening the realization of the meaning as it has been explained:
"Because the Self consists of the nature of eternal cognition, it is not [subject to] factors of action and the like; the Śruti declares, 'Not gross,' 'Not this, not this,' and 'It is not born. (113)

Because this entire dualistic expansion, beginning with the subject (grāhaka), cannot establish itself since it has as its sole material cause the non-comprehension of the Self, and because the establishment of the Self is not something that can be produced; therefore, if the intellect, the body, pots, and so forth are excluded from the Self, they should be understood as being, in the ultimate sense, like the objects of the sixth [sense].
If the intellect, body, pot, and so forth are excluded from the Self, they should be understood as being, in the ultimate sense, like the objects of the sixth [sense]. (114)
From what logical ground is this ascertained? Because:

"Depending upon consciousness—which is eternal, self-established, and immutable—the cognitions of the intellects are established; and depending upon those [cognitions], jars and other objects are established. (115)

Since the self’s status as an agent, its activity, and its fruit cannot be established by any reasoning whatsoever, it follows that this entire cycle of worldly existence—consisting of action, agent, and fruit—is nothing but a false superimposition (mithyādhyāsa) of "I-ness," "mine-ness," effort, desire, and so forth, upon the aforementioned Self. This superimposition arises solely from the failure to understand the true nature of the reality of the Self, just as the superimposition of dust, smoke, frost, mist, or blueness occurs in the sky. To establish this point, he says: "Afflicted by the false accusation of 'I,' the Self, desiring to know that [truth], took recourse in the Śruti; by that [Śruti] it was told 'not this, not this,' and thus attained absolute isolation (kaivalya). (116)
For this seeker of liberation, from these Vedic words, there arises this certain valid knowledge, just as sleep is dispelled by the sight of a dream-omen:
"I am not, nor is there anything 'mine,' for I am by nature eternally devoid of the non-Self;
just as darkness is [dispelled] in the sun, so too are superimposition and its negation with respect to me. (117)
Thus, having realized the Self whose nature has been explained in this way, he feels compassion [for others]:
"Did I not hear that Veda which, with its solemnity, proclaims 'But where' (Taitt. Up. 2.6) and thereby dispels the entire duality along with transmigratory existence? (118)
Thus, having realized the Self as "Om," he is partless, a non-doer, and actionless;
like one who is dispassionate, he has attained solitude from the intellect and other faculties.
Thus ends the second chapter. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.

I have already established through numerous arguments that this entire world—characterized by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the acts of knowing (*pramiti*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is nothing but false superimposition (*mithyādhyāsa*). Furthermore, it has been made clear that the Self (*ātman*) is immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*), devoid of the six modifications of existence such as birth and so forth. And between these two—the false superimposition and the immutable Self—there can be no connection except through ignorance (*ajñāna*), other than in cases established by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), such as: "This very [earth] is the *ṛc*, she is the fire, she is the *sāman*."

Furthermore, since that ignorance cannot have its cause in itself alone, it must be admitted that it arises in someone with respect to some object. In this context, two categories of entities have been determined: the Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman). Of these, the non-Self has no connection whatsoever with ignorance; for its very nature is ignorance itself, and it is not possible for ignorance to belong to ignorance by its own nature. Even if ignorance were to exist within that which is of the nature of ignorance, what further excellence or distinction could it produce?

Furthermore, there is no attainment of knowledge therein by which ignorance—defined as the negation of that knowledge—could exist. This is because the non-self (*anātman*) is produced from ignorance; for it is not possible for a substratum (*āśraya*) that has already been established to possess a dependent (*āśrayin*) that is to be established through the acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*). Moreover, such a [non-self] would lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) if it were independent of that [ignorance]. For these very reasons, one should understand that ignorance whose object is the non-self is impossible. Thus, first of all, the non-self is not the ignorant agent, nor is there ignorance having it as its object.

By process of elimination, let ignorance belong to the Self alone, because we observe the experience, "I am ignorant," and because of the Vedic scripture: "O Venerable One, I am indeed a knower of the mantras, but not a knower of the Self."

Furthermore, the Self cannot have ignorance as its intrinsic nature, because its essential nature is pure consciousness; nor can there be any loss of knowledge for it, since the attainment of knowledge is possible due to its being the agent of knowing. Nor is it logical that the Self is the effect of ignorance, because the immutable Self is established by its own nature independently of ignorance. Thus, it is the Self itself that is ignorant. But what is the object of that ignorance of the Self? We reply: it has the Self itself as its object.

[Objection: But surely, since the Self also has the nature of knowledge, is non-different [from it], and because of such reasons as having knowledge as its very essence (*prakṛti*), ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not possible at all. [Reply: It is indeed possible. How so? Because the distinction of that [Self] is caused solely by ignorance, just as the nature of a snake [is attributed] to a rope. Therefore, when that [ignorance] is removed, there is an absence of the evil of duality. And the removal of that [ignorance] occurs only through the Great Sentence (*vākya*) for one who knows the meaning of the words *tat* and *tvam*. Hence, this chapter is commenced for the purpose of explaining that sentence. In this regard, one who has performed the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) concerning the words and their meanings contained in sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) [proceeds as follows].
When one realizes "I am Brahman" through such [teachings] as "That thou art," then, with the notions of "I" and "mine" utterly destroyed, one no longer follows the path of speech and mind.

At the very moment one understands the meaning of "thou" as being the meaning of "that," it immediately attains the state of being the non-sentential meaning (avākyārtha) and no longer enters the path of speech and mind. On what basis is this determined? Because: "That-word" refers to the subject matter at hand [Brahman], and the "thou-word" refers to the inner self (pratyagātman).
Through these two, just as in the case of "blue lotus," the states of suffering and non-selfhood are excluded. (Verse 2)

Thus, it has been stated that one who has established the method of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) understands the meaning of the sentence from the sentence itself; therefore, the aphorism is presented for its explanation:

"Co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā), and the relationship between the indicated and the indicator (lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-sambandha) [apply] to the word-meanings and the inner Self (pratyagātman). (Verse 3)

When this Sūtra has been presented, someone raises an objection: "Regarding this method characterized by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which was stated in the preceding chapter for the sake of comprehending the meaning of the [scriptural] statements and which is preceded by the renunciation of all actions—is this brought about by an injunction, or does a person engage in it spontaneously? What follows from this? Listen.

If this method is prescribed by injunction for the direct realization of the reality of the Self, then, for the sake of that realization, one must—with the accumulation of auspicious and inauspicious karma set aside, and with a one-pointed mind—perceive the Self through the aforementioned methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Failing to complete the perception of the Self and falling away from it, one becomes "one who has fallen from what was ascended. However, if one proceeds by mere chance, then there is no fault. We say it is "prescribed by injunction" because it is said:
"One who possesses the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, shall directly perceive the Self within the self."
Having completely abandoned the sphere of "you" (the ego) through both positive and negative concomitance.
When the object "you" has been discarded by the previously stated reasons, the Śruti, out of friendship, speaks the truth—"Who am I?"—to him who has become filled with wonder. || 5 ||

Regarding this, the Sāṃkhyas raise an objection: "The false cognition that takes the body, senses, mind, and intellect—which are not the Self—to be the Self is ignorance (*ajñāna*), bound by which the Self becomes connected to manifold evils. Since that [ignorance] is dispelled precisely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it follows that statements such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*) would have no object. Therefore, the greatness of the sentence lies in this very distinction between the Self and the non-Self. To refute that, it is said:
"This knowledge is the cognition of difference, and the absence of difference resides in the Witness (*sākṣin*)."
This is the function of ignorance; one should cause it to be abandoned by means of the knowledge of the Self. || 6 ||
Having heard the statement, "One should cause [the Self] to be abandoned by means of knowledge," someone says:

"Since there is no lack of awareness of the Self other than false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), what is it that is removed by the sentence? For ignorance is indeed the absence of knowledge; and since it is non-substantial (*avastu*) by nature, how can it be the cause of transmigratory existence? For the arising of the existent from the non-existent is not accepted, as the Śruti says: 'But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? and 'How could the existent be born from the non-existent? To this it is replied:
"Because every object is indeed unknown prior to the birth of cognition."
Therefore, being existent as one alone, it remains both existent and yet unknown.
It was stated in the preceding verse that "it exists yet is unknown.
In response to the inquiry as to what this "existing yet unknown" is, he speaks in order to establish its essential nature:
"That which shines forth spontaneously when there is a desire to know, within both the knower and the means of knowledge..."
And that which is established by its own greatness should be understood as having an unknown object. || 8 ||
Regarding this, some say: whatever sentence there is here, whether worldly or Vedic, all of it conveys a sentence-meaning that consists solely of a relation (*saṃsarga*).

Therefore, having understood from sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) the sentence-meaning consisting of a relation—namely, "I am Brahman"—one should meditate upon it until the realization whose nature is the non-relational sentence-meaning, directed toward the inner self, arises in the form "I am Brahman.
From that very knowledge one attains liberation; to refute this, the following is said:
Just as there is no direct sentence-meaning for "pot" and "other than pot" due to their mutual exclusion despite grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
so too there would be no direct sentence-meaning for us regarding the referents of "That" and "Thou."

If it is asked, "From where is the meaning of the sentence determined?", the answer is that the statement regarding the competency of the qualifier and the qualified is for the purpose of understanding that [sentence-meaning].
The state of being free from suffering belongs to the referent of "thou" (tvam) because it is qualified by the referent of "that" (tat);
and the inwardness of the referent of "that" [is known] because of its proximity to this [referent of "thou"] through the word "thou. (10)

Having briefly explained grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), he now speaks in order to explain the definition and the thing defined: "The immutably conscious nature of the Self is itself the causeless ground for both the state of being a cognizer and the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*); therefore, it is characterized by those two. (11)

Regarding the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the cause of the immutable consciousness and inwardness [of the Self], there are two uncommon attributes: the state of being a knower (*boddhṛtā*) and inwardness (*apratyakṣatva*). A specific statement concerning these two is as follows:
The state of being a knower is the state of agency (*kartṛtā*) belonging to the intellect; through the sense of "I" (*ahantā*), it becomes the object (*karmatā*).
Just as there was previously a unity between those two [agency and objectivity] in the intellect, so too is there a unity of those two in the Self. (12)

Just as [the distinction between] the two prior [states] was established in the case of the intellect (*buddhi*), so too it is extended to the self (*ātman*). Since this establishes a similarity with the intellect, there arises the possibility of [thinking they are] distinct; therefore, he speaks in order to refute that: "The distinction between property and substrate belongs to this [intellect], but that does not belong to the self at all.
Therefore, the inner light [of the self] is non-different, because a cause for distinction is impossible. (13)

Showing that there is no possibility of a cause for such a distinction, he says: "In no state whatsoever is a difference observed between consciousness and subjectivity, nor is any deviation seen, just as [no difference is ever seen] between 'I' and its knower. (14)
Since this distinction belongs only to the intellect, which has ignorance as its material cause, and not to the Self, therefore this is established:
the non-duality of the innermost Self (pratyagātman) with immutable consciousness is immediate;
for, compared to immutable consciousness, this intellect, as a knower, is by its very nature perishable. (15)
Now, the characteristics of the very subject under discussion—the transforming [nature] and the immutable—are stated:
That whose essential nature is perceived by means of the valid cognition of recognition (pratyabhijñā), depending upon some particularity, is transforming, like the body. (16)

He who exists by his own majesty alone through both the universal and the particular, remains unchanging even upon emerging from [meditative absorption], like the space within a jar and so forth. || 17 ||
The nature of the Self and the intellect as the conscious inner self has been stated; now, in order to declare their respective unique characteristics, he says:
That which is the inner-self-nature of the intellect would be due to its dependence on the body and other limiting adjuncts;
but that which is the essential nature of the Self is like the emptiness of the sky. (18)
Its status as a cognizer is likewise due to its being the cause for the arising of cognition;
however, the true nature of the self remains as if stationary, like a mountain. (19)
He states that for these two—the immutable and the transforming—the cause of their relationship is precisely the non-apprehension of their true nature; no real relationship whatsoever is possible.
"This very intellect is divided by correctness, doubt, and error.
Through delusion, the states of rejection and acquisition are superimposed upon the Seer (the Self) regarding these [states of the intellect]. (20)
If it is asked, "How is the existence of the immutable Self established?"—

it is because neither destruction occurs merely by the act of destroying, nor does emergence occur merely by the act of arising; rather, its establishment must occur in that which is devoid of such [change], being characterized by neither loss nor gain.
Thus,
having shaken off all that is non-self by means of the two reasons— coming and going—
the [mahāvākya] "That thou art" destroys the innate darkness within the "I."

This and more is stated repeatedly because the brevity of the text is intended to facilitate the clarity of understanding. In this regard, although from such sentences as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) the meaning of being remote and dualistic is perceived—just like the intended meaning of the non-dual Self—nevertheless, that [dualistic] meaning is not what the Śruti intends to convey through its primary purport (*tātparya*), since it has already been discarded by prior cognition.
With this point in mind, he says: "In common usage, the word *tat* (That) conveys many meanings."
Without abandoning its indirectness, that [cognition] arises solely from the denotative function [of words]. || 23 ||
Similarly, even the word "thou" (tvam) directly denotes the sense of the pure subject;
yet, without abandoning its state as a transmigrating being, it too arises from verbal designation.
He states that because they are contradictory to what is being designated (*uddeśana*), invisibility (*pārokṣya*) and suffering (*duḥkhitva*) are not intended to be expressed:
"That which is being designated within a sentence does not possess the qualities of the designation; it enters into a connection with the meaning of the word that is required [by it]. (25)

Since this is so, the conclusion is that even though the meanings of *tat* and *tvam* are not intended to be grasped [as separate entities], their relationship as qualifier and qualified serves solely to indicate the meaning of the sentence as being devoid of difference or connection:
"Therefore, *tat* has the sense of a qualifier and *tvam* has the sense of the qualified;
between those two and the inner self (pratyagātman), there would be a relationship of the indicated and the indicator. (26)
But how can that which is being discarded as unintended and contradictory serve as a definition?
Just as a rope is defined by its resemblance to a snake, so too is the Inner Self (pratyak) [defined] by the "I" (aham);
for one understands the meaning of the sentence precisely through the sublation of that [notion], since it too rests upon that [Inner Self]. (27)
And this comprehension of the meaning of the sentence belongs only to one who is proficient in positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); for:
"To whatever extent this [inquirer] rejects the body and so forth, he turns inward toward the inner self."
To that same extent, the meaning of "That" (tad-artha) also seeks to enter into the meaning of "Thou" (tvam-artha). || 28 ||

For what reason, then, does the Self identify itself as the Self for the sake of that [body and so forth] only when the body and other such things are realized to be non-Self, and not the reverse? It is said in reply: Because the non-realization of the inner Self (pratyagātman) has the nature of being non-Self, this entire complex beginning with the intellect (buddhi) and ending with the body is produced from that [non-realization]. Within that, the status of being the Self is created by ignorance alone; even the status of being non-Self belongs only to one who possesses ignorance. Since the wise one, free from ignorance, remains as the absolute, solitary reality which is the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), it is therefore said: "Because of the intervention of the body and so forth, for its sake, he himself [identifies with it]."
One knows that non-self only through mediation; its directness is [the realization of] that very self. (29)
The employment of an illustration is for the sake of making easy the comprehension of the meaning as it has been stated:
"Just as for one whose internal bile has arisen, external objects appear yellow, so too does the consciousness belonging to the inner self appear as if it were external. (30)
Therefore, let it be understood that [the meaning] is thus purified:

"For by extracting words from sentences through positive and negative concomitance, and having understood the word-meanings from common worldly usage, one easily understands the sentence-meaning. (31)
But how can a word, which functions only with respect to a universal, be the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning? Very well;
for a word expresses the universal, while the particular is brought about by the sentence.
A word becomes meaningful in its specific sense when it is connected with direct audition (*śruti*) and other such factors. (32)

He states that it is the sentence itself—preceded by the methods of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka) and through the dissolution of the veil of ignorance via grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and so forth—that consecrates the seeker of liberation in self-sovereignty; for this goal cannot be accomplished by the method of agreement and difference alone:
"The non-selfhood of the intellect and other faculties is established even by inference; yet, liberation does not result from that alone.
Therefore, one must rely upon the [great] sentence [of the Upanishads]. (33)
He says that not only does one who relies solely on inference fail to attain the desired goal, but he also incurs misfortune:
"Therefore, out of delusion, disregarding the Śruti, the dark-minded Buddhists—who have inference as their sole eye—fell into the doctrine of selflessness (nirātmatva). (34)

Nor is there any reason for disregard, because in every case the grounds for disregard regarding a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) consist in its merely restating what is already apprehended by another means of knowledge, or its presenting something contrary, or its presenting something doubtful, or its not presenting anything at all—and none of these reasons is present here.
As it has been said:
"The Self, which is free from suffering and not grasped by other means of knowledge, [is presented] directly..."
Since the Veda brings about awakening, why is it not said to be a means of valid cognition? || 35 ||

Nor does it cause one to understand by means of doubt; for: "Since every cause of doubt has been discarded, how could doubt arise regarding the self from a statement addressed to 'you' (the listener) through inference? (36)
Moreover: That regarding which there might be doubt cannot be known as the Self by the wise; for no doubt can arise concerning the Self, because it is of the nature of pure awareness. (37)
The charge of being unintelligible is utterly dismissed; for it has been said:
"How can a scripture enlighten one in whom no experience whatsoever arises even upon hearing? It would be like trying to teach a clod of earth that merely has the shape of a man. (38)

To strengthen this position—that it is the sentence itself, preceded by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that establishes the self in the form of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—he presents an example from the Śruti:
"That which knows 'I am smelling this odor,' being itself changeless—that is the Self; that is the supreme light. This is the statement found at the beginning of the Śruti. (39)

Just as the scriptural passages on positive and negative concomitance—beginning with "This person who is seen in the eye" and ending with "Now, he who knows 'I shall smell this'"—are supplementary to the statement "That is the Truth, That is the Self, Thou art That," so too are they supplementary to the realization "I am Brahman.

For the Śruti, having eliminated all sense of "Thou" (the external), repeatedly declares through the words "This which... and so forth that the meaning of "I" is the innermost Self (pratyagātman). (40)
How, then, is this meaning determined—that here, under the guise of "I," the reality of the Self is intended to be made known? Because:
"This Self is self-luminous; when the sun, moon, fire, and speech have set, it remains as if sightless, yet it continues to illumine the activity of the mind. (41)
And when questioned, the sage explained:
having heard the words "by the self alone," and upon the inquiry "What is this self?
the sage declared that the self is beyond the intellect and is by its very nature liberated. (42)

And because the inner self alone is intended to be made known under the guise of the "I," therefore the mental modification (*ahaṃvṛtti*) attains the status of being the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence only through the dissolution of its own form; he states this point as follows:
"Since this [person] understands that Brahman by means of the very modification 'I,' therefore the ego-function (*ahaṃkṛti*) must be the cause through the dissolution of its own nature. (43)
For this very reason, the point which was proposed—"I am neither the object of perception nor that which is devoid of it," and so forth—being established by logical arguments, is now concluded:
"If the referent of the word 'I' were grasped [as an object], why would the Knower not realize [itself]?

If you say it is because of contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, then the statement regarding the Inner Self (Pratīc) does not fall within the domain of 'you' (the empirical subject). (44)
To clarify the meaning of the preceding verse, he says:

"But all means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, are directed only toward the external and not toward the Self; whereas the statement 'That thou art' is directly engaged with that which is inward. (45)

Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one should extract the Self from the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—which are respectively rejected and accepted—and, like the stalk from the *muñja* grass, discern the Self as the witness of all modifications of the intellect. One should know the Self, characterized as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth, through such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*). This very point is stated: "That by which this unstable cognition—'I am miserable,' 'I am happy'—appears until its culmination in pure awareness, that is my Self. This is the wisdom arising from the Great Sentence (*vākya-dhī*). (46)

It has been stated repeatedly that sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) indeed directly and immediately establish—like a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of one's hand—the Self, which is not grasped by other means of knowledge, which has all duality consisting of cause and effect entirely sublated, and which is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; they do so by way of destroying doubt, false knowledge, and ignorance.

Regarding this, some say: "The aforementioned meaning cannot be understood through sentences such as 'That thou art,' because they are restricted to the restatement of the true nature of things exactly as they exist, and because they are merely verbal testimony (*abhidhā-śruti*)."

For in the world, the validity of a verbal statement such as "There are fruits on the riverbank," which is independent of other means of knowledge, is not accepted. Therefore, it is logical that the validity of a verbal statement derives solely from the *niyoga* (injunction), because the *niyoga* is independent of other means of knowledge. To refute this [objection], this [section] begins with the aim of establishing that the validity of the verbal statement arises from its having as its object supersensuous matters (*atīndriyārtha*) by way of negating that it is an object of perception and the rest of the means of knowledge; thus, its validity must be stated to be like that of a sentence awakening a sleeping person. This is because it consists of eternal cognition and does not depend on any other measure.
Because it is devoid of qualities such as sound and because no doubt can arise regarding it. || 47 ||
The self is not cognized through perception and other means by means of spitting out craving;
for it is the inner self, because it is one's own purpose, and because it is not an object of measurement.
Scripture also declares this same point:

"Because it relies upon forms and other qualities that are limited and intended for the gaze of others, one does not see that which is self-awakened through vision, as it is perceived in its opposite. (49)
Therefore, the Śruti, as a means of valid knowledge, respectfully declares that which is established by logic: one cannot perceive the inner self, the seer of the self's vision. (50)
Another reason for [the self] not being an object of inference is stated:
since perception is directed outward, it cannot grasp the relation [of the self];
therefore, there can be no experience of this [self] through inference whatsoever. (51)

Thus, this entire empirical transaction consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge pertains exclusively to external objects; it is not capable of penetrating the internal Self.
And this being so, he says that the aforementioned matter can indeed be understood by means of this very [transaction]:
"This entire empirical transaction of the means of knowledge pertains to that which is external."
Therefore, even after careful consideration, he desires to see you alone.

Since the meaning of the sentence "I am Brahman" is not accessible through worldly means of knowledge such as perception and the like, therefore, for the seeker who has attained the vision [of truth] after having discarded [the notion of the self] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) starting from the vital breaths, the Śruti proclaimed: "Who am I? and "That thou art. (53)

This very logic of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) extends only so far as to culminate in the realization of the meaning of the sentence, which dawns upon one who understands it as "I am Brahman.

This is stated concisely according to the acceptance of the Śruti, by means of the distinction between the seer and the seen, and the distinction between the witness and that which arises and perishes:
"Because it is an object of sight, the body is like a pot; and the sense organs are likewise like the body."
The mind should be understood as being like the sense organs; like the mind, it possesses the capacity for determination and so forth.
Likewise, by being the witness to the division of all effects and causes as they arise and pass away—
that which was previously non-existent attains existence, and that which exists likewise returns to non-existence—
it must be without self-origination; its opposite, however, is the Self-luminous Vision (dṛśi).

In this regard, the non-selfhood of perceptible objects such as jars is first apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, preceded by the perceiver who is the Self. Having determined the specific attributes of that which is not the Self, one excludes the functions of the body, senses, mind, and the process of determination as being non-self by means of those attributes—such as perceptibility and the qualities of coming into and passing out of existence. Then, because even the function of "I" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*) is equally perceptible, it is concluded that it too must be preceded by a perceiver, the Self. This is what is stated [in the verse]:
"Just as jars and the like are signs (*liṅga*) of the 'I' through a traditional succession, so too the 'I' is a sign of the perceiving Self, because of its perceptibility. (56)

[Objection: But surely, since the seer, the seeing, and the seen are observed to appear and disappear during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, that witness of their appearance and disappearance—the Self which is devoid of the distinction between appearance and disappearance—is like the sun, which is devoid of the distinction between light and darkness, for it is upon its basis that the world’s manifestation and non-manifestation depend. And if this is so, then since the object to be understood from the sentence has already been apprehended through inference alone—being of the nature of pure consciousness that neither rises nor sets—the sentence would again face the contingency of being rendered purposeless. [Reply: This is not a fault.

Because that realization occurs through the mediation of an inferential mark (*liṅga*). [Objection: But since one grasps the relationship between the abandonment and acquisition of the non-self by means of the very nature of the Self—which is immediate and non-mediated—what excellence could a sentence possibly effect? [Response: Do not speak thus; for that realization is dependent upon an inferential mark.

Indeed, the realization of the Self through the mediation of an inferential mark does not constitute immediate realization, according to the Vedic scripture: "He is to be obtained only by the one whom He chooses. Therefore, he says:
Because an indicator (liṅga) is restricted to existence, it cannot convey the meaning of a sentence;
therefore, from the sentence, this Self is understood as being beyond both existence and non-existence.

Now, if you maintain that the reality intended by your statement is a thing from which the entire web of conceptual constructions regarding existence and non-existence has been excluded, nevertheless, the thirst for the subject matter of such a statement is dispelled. This is because the reality—devoid of all conceptual constructions—is established even without hearing a statement, as it is evident to everyone from cowherds and shepherds to scholars during deep sleep; therefore, there is no purpose in hearing a statement. This is not so.

What is the reason? Because the non-apprehension of the Self, which is the seed of all misfortune, exists in deep sleep. For if ignorance did not exist in deep sleep, then even for all living beings, the cessation of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence would follow by its own force, simply from the realization "I am Brahman" arising from the hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration upon the Vedāntic texts. Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a rising again from the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), as that would entail the impossibility of final release.

Nor can it be said that the one who was asleep is entirely different from the one who has awakened, because we observe recognition upon waking, such as: "I did not perceive anything else at all while I was asleep. Therefore, ignorance must necessarily be admitted to exist during deep sleep. [Objection: But if ignorance were present there, it would have been perceived directly—just like desire, hatred, or the ignorance regarding a pot—as in this world, where the immediate ignorance expressed as "I do not know the pot" is directly perceived. [Reply: This is not so, because of the absence of a manifesting agent (*abhivyañjaka*).
If you ask how there is an absence of a manifesting agent, listen:

Just as the manifestation of the "I" (aham) does not occur without producing an external mental state, so too the clear manifestation of darkness does not occur without the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). 58.

Someone, recollecting what has been passed over, says that it was stated without logical justification: "Because it is visible, the *liṅga* (the subtle body) would likewise be the sign of the seeing Self. What is the reason? Because the distinction between the "I" (*ahaṃ*) and its knower is not established. Just as in this world the distinction between a jar and Devadatta as the object of perception and the perceiver is very clearly established, there is no such distinction here between the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and its knower; therefore, what was stated is incorrect. To this it is replied:
"Just as there may be the relationship of the combustible and the combustor in one and the same place for fire and wood..."
In this way, there would be a mutual relationship of object and subject between the "I" and the knower. (59)

Thus, first of all, the function of "I" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*) operates for the sake of delimiting the internal organ—which has arisen from ignorance—by means of the form of external objects. Being delimited by that [function], it attains the status of an object through its immediate proximity to the nature of the awareness that constitutes the substrate (*upādāna*) of the immutable inner self (*kūṭastha-pratyagātman*). In this regard, no other relationship between those two—the knower in the form of the "I-notion" and the illuminator—is possible, apart from the relationship between the illuminator and the illuminated.

Having made the form of egoity its own and having donned the cloak of egoity (*ahaṃkaraṇa*), it becomes capable of being either a beneficiary or a benefactor; thus, through an external object—whether beneficial or harmful—it establishes a relationship between the self and what belongs to the self.
This is stated as follows:
"This knowledge would belong to the knower; likewise, 'my knowledge' belongs to the ego."
Due to the limiting adjunct of ignorance, this sense of "I" and "mine" arises from the modification [of the intellect].
It has been stated that even when the object is distinct due to the difference between internal and external causes, a cognition of two forms arises for a single knower in the form of "this is mine.
Here, how is it understood that the notion of "mine" occurs toward an object for a knower who is being benefited or harmed, whereas in the opposite case, the notion of "this" occurs?
Let it be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). To explain how this is so, he says:
Because it is not being acted upon, there can be no "I" or "mine" for the knower;
however, this [notion] occurs like a jar or other objects, depending solely upon delusion.

Because ignorance and its effects are the substratum for both the state of being a knower and modification, the connection with the notions of "this" and "mine" was previously demonstrated [in the waking state]. Now, however, he speaks in order to demonstrate their absence through their negation [in deep sleep]: "Because it is devoid of modification and cognition, this is not mine, nor am I [the agent] of the Self;
for when one has awakened, there is the realization: 'I did not know anything. (62)
In order to demonstrate the extent of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, he says:
"The full measure of this [discrimination] is understood through both verbal testimony and direct perception;
yet the destruction of that delusion which produces misfortune occurs from the Word alone concerning the eternally existent Self. (63)
At the beginning of the second chapter, four types of listeners were presented.

Among them, for one who—upon the cessation of the entire non-Self—realizes the state of being the meaning of the sentence within the inner Self (pratyagātman), all causes of internal obstacles have been exhausted; thus, nothing whatsoever remains to be said to him. Furthermore, even for one who realizes it merely by hearing the sentence, there is nothing further to be required, owing to his possession of extraordinary power (atīndriya-śaktimat).

Furthermore, one who has been made to hear such sentences as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and so forth, and who, having himself performed the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), realizes the meaning of the sentence at its very conclusion—such a person also has realized the truth exactly as it is, and like the previous case, he is to be disregarded [as requiring no further instruction].

But as for one who, even after being made to perform the method of agreement and difference, is made to hear the sentence again and again for the sake of realizing the reality as it is—for such a person who has already performed the agreement and difference, why is the sentence heard? It is said in reply:
"Just as one whose cognition was captivated by the number nine perceives the tenth person through delusion..."
Even while looking at those nine, the tenth does not know, "I am the tenth."
Now, intending to apply the meaning found in the illustration to the subject of the illustration, he says:

"Even one who has cast off duality does not, in this way, know the non-dual Self without [the instruction] 'That thou art' and so forth; nor is there any need for further investigation into the cause of this. (65)
It has been stated that no further reason need be sought here; when asked why that is, he replies: "Because it cannot withstand investigation. How so? He says:
This delusion is without foundation and contradicts all logic;
it cannot endure inquiry, just as darkness cannot endure the sun. (66)

Indeed, the cessation of this very ignorance, which is error, occurs through the arising of right knowledge; and the firm destruction of one’s desire to know [the Self] is achieved by means of such [scriptural passages] as "That thou art. Realization of the Inner Self (Pratyak) must come about in this way; it cannot arise from any other means of valid cognition.
If it is asked how a sentence indeed brings about comprehension, the answer is the statement of an illustration:
Just as for one who desires to know the tenth man and is distressed after passing over the nine, the words "You yourself are the tenth" produce certain knowledge; so too does a sentence. (68)
And that [knowledge] arises precisely because it is produced by the valid cognition born from hearing such statements as "That thou art.
Nor does another cognition arise to the effect that "it is not so. He illustrates this very point with an example:
"The cognition arising from the sentence 'You are the tenth' is not sublated for him."
He has no doubt regarding these nine [stages] in their beginning, middle, and end. || 69 ||
Thus, from the statement "That thou art," which dispels duality regarding the inner self, there arises a firm valid cognition once the meaning of "thou" has been correctly understood. (70)
It has been stated that valid cognition (*pramā*) arises with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*); regarding this, an objection is raised:

Does valid cognition arise with respect to the inner self as the agent, just as valid cognition regarding objects of knowledge such as a jar arises without the negation of the distinctions between the various factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the agent? Or does it arise through the complete sublation of the entire collection of factors of action? The reply is: Its nature as the inner self (*pratyaktā*) is intrinsic; it is devoid of action, devoid of factors of action, and devoid of fruit.
That intellect, ignited by that [light], appears as non-dual, just like the inner self (pratyagātman). || 71 ||
Since this is so,
even the wise extend their self-identity toward that [mind],
for it diminishes further and further with respect to the objects of the senses as they become more remote. (72)

He says: If words alone are what bring about the understanding of things as they truly are, then for what reason is there the teaching of agency and so forth, which are produced by ignorance? To this objection, the following reply is given: Having restated an object established through delusion, one teaches its true nature by subverting that delusion, saying "this is not so"; and in the same way, one teaches that "such is the reality. (73)
He brings this point to mind through an illustration:
"The statement 'a post, a post' does not eliminate the cognition of a person;
likewise, a statement that merely repeats [what is already perceived] does not sublate a person's error. (74)

Since the word *tvam* (you) merely restates what is already established for the listener, its status as a subject (*uddiśyamāna*) implies that qualities such as suffering are not intended to be predicated (*avivakṣitatva*).

For while a contradiction may arise when two things are both being predicated (*vidhīyamāna*), there is no such contradiction between that which is being predicated and that which is being restated. Indeed, the suspicion of contradiction arises only between two words that are primary (*svapradhāna*), because they possess common gender and number; this does not apply to their opposite case. When these two [words] are not governed by common gender and number, they do not express anything to be abandoned.
Having emerged from that state, those two then looked at one another.

If it is argued: "Let there indeed be no connection between the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*, since [the former] has its general sense discarded, since it resides in a restatement (*anuvāda*), and because it contradicts that which is being enjoined; let there likewise be no connection with the suffering and so forth [of the latter] as they are objects to be abandoned. However, let there be a connection between the meanings of *tat* and *tvam* like 'blue lotus,' as this avoids the faults previously mentioned"—this is not tenable even thus. Therefore: "But the ultimate reality of those two meanings is the Self, devoid of duality and remoteness.
There is no non-dual [reality] without the Self, nor is there a Self without the eternally perceiving consciousness. (76)
Here it is asked: "What is it that is to be abandoned here, or what is it that is to be acquired? It is replied:

From the term *tvaṃ* (thou), which denotes the inner self (*pratyagātman*), two things are perceived—the "I who am suffering" and the "inner self. And therein, the connection of the inner self with the notion "I am suffering" is caused solely by the failure to realize the true nature of the Self. Therefore, the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) is to be abandoned because it is adventitious and born of ignorance; this is known through direct perception. However, it is not yet determined what among its objects is to be abandoned and what is to be acquired. Consequently, this is stated:

That which is the state of being remote (pārokṣya) in relation to that object [the Self] should be abandoned, just like the "I-sense" (ahamartha); for just as there is no difference between the "I" and consciousness, so too there is no difference between the "I" and the Self in its state of remoteness.

But how does that meaning, characterized by non-duality, remove the state of having a second and the state of being a sufferer—which have their locus in the inner self—without leaving a trace? It is said in reply: we do not say that there is a relationship of sublater and sublated between these two. How then?
Non-duality, which was previously unperceived in the inner self—the referent of "thou"—is made known by this [instruction].

Therefore, by the removal of non-comprehension, there is no occasion for objections such as "lack of grammatical coreferentiality" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), since that which arises from it—the state of having a second (*sadvitīyatva*)—is removed along with the referent of *tvam* (the individual self) and the state of being remote (*parokṣatva*) residing in the referent of *tat*. This is stated as follows:

"When joined with the meaning of *tat*, [the meaning of *tvam*] eliminates plurality; the meaning of *tvam*, without having abandoned its remoteness, does not seek to merge into the meaning of *tat*. (78)

But for what reason does that meaning, characterized by non-duality, being distinct in its referent from the "thou" (tvam) as the inner self (pratyagātman), destroy the state of having a second which arises from ignorance? It is said: because of contradiction. This is explained:
"The state of being a transmigrator and the remoteness [of the 'that'] are adventitious;
because they are contradictory, they are sublated by the two terms 'That' and 'Thou'. (79)
Furthermore, another reason for the sublation of the meanings of "That" and "Thou" is stated:

because the meaning of "That" is not known as a human goal and because it is derived from scripture, these two contradictory meanings may act as sublaters without abandoning their own respective referents. (80)

Thus, first of all, according to the method of exposition as it has been introduced, not even a scent of contradiction with other means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, can be imagined.

However, when we strive in every possible way and still do not find this meaning of the sentence tenable—precisely because of its contradiction with other means of valid cognition such as perception—it is said regarding that position:
"If a sentence were to express a meaning somewhere that contradicts perception and the rest..."
But it may well be for the purpose of enjoining that vision [of Brahman], as in the case of the woman and the fire; of this there is no doubt. (81)

But when a sentence such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), even upon being investigated in every possible way, does not glance even with a sidelong look toward action, then the operation of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) and the like becomes impossible. This is stated [in the verse]:
If a sentence were to have as its sole objective a real entity (*vastu*), it could not have action as its purpose.
For since a real entity possesses a single, uniform nature, there is no possibility of alternative options (*vikalpa*) regarding it. (82)
Furthermore, because their objects are distinct, there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How so?
It is said: A [cognition] would be a means of valid cognition if it brings about the apprehension of what was previously unknown; if it does not, it is not one.
Therefore, no contradiction is logical between two [cognitions] that apprehend different objects. || 83 ||
Whoever asserts a contradiction between these [senses] despite their having different objects would likewise have to assert a contradiction here as well:
"This is not sound, because I see form with my eye"—just as that, such is the contradiction between the sensory perception and the verbal statement. (84)

There is no contradiction between existing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they have different objects, just like the ear and other senses. And for those two that have the same object, there would indeed be a relationship of sublated and sublator, as in the case of the rat and the mongoose. Therefore, it is said: "If it is perception, it cannot be verbal; if it is verbal, how could it be born of the senses?"
For pseudo-perception occurs within perception, and pseudo-scripture occurs within scripture. (85)
Furthermore, the logic of the thesis, reason, and example is not applicable here, because sound and the other means of knowledge each function as an independent authority; therefore, he says:
"The means of knowledge bring about the comprehension of objects by their own power; validity is not held to be [established] through mutual assistance, for it is intrinsic. (86)

Furthermore, the connection of the self with pleasure, pain, and so forth is not apprehended by means of perception and other valid cognitions (pramāṇas) in such a way that a contradiction with those pramāṇas would be exposed. If the cognition of being a sufferer were [itself] a valid cognition, it could not be known [by another], just like the self;
for validity is rightly attributed only to the object of cognition, and never to the agent of cognition. (87)
Moreover, even if you were to accept [this], you could not be freed from the faults that have been imputed to you even by a hundred meditations (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Therefore, he says:
"Since it is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by what can this state of suffering be warded off?
If its cessation were like the heat of fire, then indeed one would fall into the Buddhist doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*). (88)

Now, if it is thought: "If discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), when properly practiced, were to eliminate the state of suffering, how could it produce valid cognition (*pramā*) given that it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge? (89)

Now, it may be argued that what is called *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is defined as the repeated mental application directed toward the meaning of words such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And this, when practiced, produces a complete realization by increasing correct knowledge (*pramiti*), rather than by increasing one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*). For example, the notion that "this is a woman" regarding a corpse in a heap of all manner of filth is a cognition produced merely by human effort, devoid of any objective basis. That is not so; for:
The very one-pointedness of the intellect that arises from the accumulation of practice is itself [the result].
For the means of valid cognition do not produce the comprehension of an object through repeated practice.
If cultivation, accumulated through practice, were to bring about the cessation of everything,
that cessation would not be absolute, for its fruit is born of cultivation.
Moreover, it is said:

"If even the notion 'I am suffering,' which has been nourished for ten million eons, can be destroyed, then what proof is there that a cultivation produced by even slight practice will not remain stable? (92)
[Objection: But surely stability will result from the scripture. [Reply: Not so;
for the scripture merely effects the comprehension of the true nature of things as they actually exist.
Scripture does not bestow power upon the capacities of objects, and this is well known in the world.
Whatever fruit may arise from meditative cultivation, and whatever fruit may arise from ritual action,
one should not consider that to be stable, just as it was understood among the Draviḍas.

Although the self's state of suffering is apprehended through means of valid cognition such as perception, nevertheless, the conviction arising from sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) alone is more powerful. This is because it originates from a statement whose validity is non-deviant, and because the object of knowledge (prameya) is established by its very nature as being free from suffering. Perception and the like, however, are subject to deviation, and mere probability is based solely on human imagination.
Thus, freedom from suffering is self-evident, whereas suffering is [apprehended] through perception and the like.
For who, disregarding their own self, would place trust in external honor? (94)
It is precisely for the sake of establishing a connection.
Furthermore, the engagement [of the senses] with the inner self occurs despite the contradiction of direct perception;
this is understood from the scriptural statement, "The sense-organs are directed outward. (95)

This is stated on the basis of a mere concession; however, we have repeatedly declared that a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not contradicted by another means of knowledge. Even where there is a suspicion of contradiction between a statement and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that suspicion arises solely through the power of human delusion and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, he says:
"If a statement were to produce a cognition that contradicts direct perception and the like..."
A wise person may speak of figurative perceptibility when the primary sense is impossible.
An illustration is given for the sake of easily understanding that meaning:
"Agni studies correctly; Mañcaka laughed loudly.
Just as in those cases, he (the Self) is indicated by the "I-notion," even though it is inappropriate [for Him]. (97)

But for what reason is the Self not denoted directly; what is the use of this conceptualization? To that he says: "Leaving aside that which is not the 'Thou', nothing else exists here that conveys the realization of the Self; yet even the referent of 'Thou' exists here by virtue of a mere fraction of its qualities. (98)

For what reason, then, does even this notion of "I" exist only through a trace of the qualities (*guṇa-leśa*) and not directly? Because the nature of the Self (*ātman*) is such that all causes for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) have been shaken off. Therefore, it is said:
Just as those of evil intellect might imagine smoke, frost, clouds, or soot in the sky, so do the deluded imagine transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) within the inner Self (*pratyagātman*). (99)

Now, since it is equally impossible for all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) to exist in the Self, what is the reason for this partiality toward the "I-notion" (*ahaṃvṛtti*), such that one discards other mental states and perceives the Self through the "I-notion" alone? It is said in reply: This "I-notion" is of the nature of consciousness, like the inner [Self], and distinct from the Self in other respects;
for the reasons stated previously, it is therefore called the Self. (100)
If the supreme Seer were indicated by mental modifications that have you as their object, then He would be non-self, and the word of the Śruti would be false. (101)

By this slight trace of quality, as previously described— namely, by the function of "I" (ahaṃ-vṛtti) which consists of the agent and the action of the "I-maker"— that [Self] is indicated; it is not directly denoted here.
If it is asked what the reason is for the fact that [the Self] is not denoted directly here, [the reply is:
"The causes for the application of words are the genitive relation, quality, action, genus, and conventional usage.
Since none of these apply to the Self, the Self is not denoted. (103)
If a word does not apply to itself by accepting the relationship between the signifier and the signified, how can the perfect realization "I am Brahman" arise from a word?
It is said in reply:
"Abiding on a false path, one reaches the goal which is beyond all means."
We know this because of our own nature, having been awakened through the functioning of the qualities.

But how can a designation, being unconnected with its designated object, produce valid knowledge regarding an object that is not [directly] designated? Listen: it is said that even though it is unconnected, it causes one to understand the non-designated object by way of dispelling ignorance: "Just as those who are lying down in the world are generally awakened at once when addressed by their own names, so too [is awakening produced] regarding the inner Self. (105)
For there is no connection with the name for one who has emerged from the body;
nevertheless, he understands through it that "the reality is just so. (106)

And just as, without touching the sky, the notions of "darkness" and "light" existing within a bird's nest would be mutually contradictory, so too should it be understood here regarding the Self. (107)
Hearing the words, “Standing on a false path,” someone, struck with great astonishment and in a state of high agitation, objects:
“No unreal means exists in this world for the ascertainment of ultimate reality;
for no one attains fire by means of an unreal sign such as steam. (108)
Even one who might raise such an objection should be satisfied by the example of a jar and so forth;
for that [entity] is distinguished from both the existent and the non-existent, and it is a mode (paryāya) that does not belong to these two.
Thus, having uprooted these frivolous objections, the subject at hand is now stated.

As for the subject at hand: how can the hearing of the verbal expression [of the Upanishads] produce knowledge that destroys ignorance regarding the Self, which is itself inexpressible? In this regard, another reason is stated:
"Ignorance is extremely difficult to dispel here, for the Self alone is its awakening."
Having perceived this as a mere sign, it is like a jujube fruit on the tip of the nose.

If it is argued that the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*) is difficult to conceive because the Self (*ātman*) is by nature nothing but immutable, ever-shining consciousness that neither rises nor sets, we say: no, for its existence is established simply by the very fact that ignorance is well-known, just as the night is established for an owl. Therefore, this is said: "O, how audacious is ignorance! No one can transcend it;
disregarding all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reality itself, it stands as if it were the Supreme Self. (111)

Since the existence of ignorance is established solely through the very fact of its being well-known [as such], there is no possibility whatsoever of its occurrence in accordance with the nature of the reality of the Self; as it is said:
"For one whose innate nature is knowledge, devoid of action and its factors, by what cause could there even be a possibility of ignorance? (112)

Thus, although this Self has as its very nature the mere realization that neither rises nor sets, it is perceived as something other than what it is, being veiled only by ignorance (avidyā) which is established through a lack of inquiry; for this reason:
"Because of this, [the Self] appears as if excluded from existence and resorted to non-existence;
therefore, for one who desires to know, its cessation [from such appearance] occurs through the sentence alone. (113)
If it is asked, "Why does cessation [of the world] not also occur through inference alone, just as it occurs from the existence [of things]? listen:

because one cannot, by means of inference, be consecrated to the sovereignty of one's own self—which is characterized by the cessation of all activity, agents, and fruits—therefore, this person is fast asleep due to the sleep of ignorance, which is difficult to discern.
By the very scripture that negates both existence and non-existence, one is awakened. || 115 ||

Here it is argued: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is difficult to conceive, because its nature consists solely of the self whose consciousness neither rises nor sets. This is not so. Why? Because it is said: "How could there be the objection 'How is there ignorance? since prior to [its existence] the cause is impossible?
And because it is not delimited by the three times, the objection cannot arise afterwards either. (116)
Since it is the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) alone that dispels the self's entire ignorance without leaving a trace, therefore:
"Those who, disregarding this most certain means of knowledge, seek to know 'Thou art That' through other means, would be attempting to perceive taste with their eyes. (117)

If it is argued that even though the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) produces the valid cognition "I am Brahman," which is thus unimpeded, it does not actually bring about realization, then realization would never occur from any source whatsoever; therefore, he says:

"If one were to say this [the Veda] is false, even when there is a true comprehension, then there would be no confidence in anything else either, for there is no difference in the nature of the comprehension. (118)

Nor is it proper to postulate another sentence-meaning from the sentence-meaning already intended to be conveyed; for: "If there were no experience [of a further meaning] even when the word-meanings have been understood, then another injunction would have to be postulated there; yet no other meaning is actually apprehended. (119)
And the intended meaning is not left unestablished by the reasoning already stated.
What is that reasoning? He says:
"Having set aside name and the rest, the referent of 'thou' (tvam-artha) is devoid of all attributes."
Free from desire for your possessions, he is impelled by the injunctions for tranquility and the other virtues. || 120 ||
Having broken those five bolts consisting of the annamaya-kośa and the others by realizing they are not the Self,
if one knows the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman," there is no further need for effort.

If it were not accepted in this way, then that which is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the sentence—would result in being non-authoritative (*aprāmāṇya*). Thus he says: "And for whatever purpose a sentence is employed, if it does not produce a cognition regarding that [purpose], by what reason could its authoritativeness be established? (122)
Now, if you think:
"If one could know [the self] through meditative discernment (prasaṃkhyāna), how could the Word be a speaker of truth?
For the Word tells us that it is beyond the senses, whereas knowledge through discernment is undoubtedly [direct]."
Nor do we consider it possible that a correct realization will arise from *prasaṃkhyāna* characterized by the repetition of reasoning and verbal instruction; for:
"If reasoning and verbal instruction did not previously produce valid cognition (pramā) regarding this [object], what unprecedented result will follow from their direct repetition? (124)
Now, if you say, "Even so, I am unable to sustain my life-breaths without continuous meditation (prasaṃkhyāna)," then we shall accomplish it through hearing (śravaṇa) and the other means alone. How?
"The same principle that applies to continuous meditation should apply to the scripture:
having heard only slightly, or having heard incompletely, one comes to understand by hearing it thoroughly. (125)

[Objection: But surely, for one who does not accept the injunction for *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment), the conduct of a *paramahaṃsa* would—like the conduct of Buddhists and others—be devoid of scriptural authority; consequently, there would be no such thing as "falling from a high station," nor would the cessation of all karmas be possible. [Reply: It is said:
Since even an injunction is resorted to for the sake of awakening to the meaning of "Thou" (*tvam*), those defects which were alleged in its absence do not arise, for they lack a cause. (126)
Thus ends the third chapter. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
That very subject which was clearly explained in detail in the preceding chapters, I shall now state in brief for the sake of easy comprehension. (1)
For when a subject is explained both concisely and in detail, it enters the inner heart of men of dull and superior intellect respectively; therefore, it is called *vastu*. (2)
In this world, both the self (ātman) and the non-self (anātman) are established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception;
however, of these two, the non-self is everywhere preceded by the self.
The selflessness of any entity distinct from the body is established by its own nature;
likewise, the knower is the Self. Between these two, a doubt is observed. (4)

Having understood their uncommon properties, the wise person, like [one inferring] smoke and fire, should then know through inference those [factors] beginning with the intellect and ending with the non-self. || 5 ||
Since this duality— namely "this" with respect to external objects and "I" with respect to the cognizer—
is perceived within the body, for that reason people are deluded.
But by what reasoning is the distinction between the Self and the non-Self made, as in the case of a horse and a buffalo? It is said:

"The reasoning that effects the distinction between the Self and the non-Self has been set forth by us previously. By means of that, having set aside this object [the 'this'], one should discern that which exists in the notion of 'I'. (7)

From the realization of "That thou art," the sage should easily and immediately perceive that which is devoid of internal and external objects, abiding within as the Self, and which is always beyond the vision of existence and non-existence.
Then, let it be stated: by what process does one understand the meaning of the sentence?
It is said: through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Because of having abandoned the entire sphere of "this-ness" (idam-artha), one thinks, "I am abandoned."
For this reason, I do not understand my own self from what is not-self.

Now, having ascertained through valid means that everything from the body up to the intellect is indeed non-self, why does one not cease from the desire to know? Listen: "As long as the desire to know the inner Self has not been severed, this person, with a mind swinging back and forth due to the non-self, becomes deluded like a materialist. (10)
Since the Self, whose nature is unimpaired consciousness, is eternally present precisely because it is the Self, why does the seeker not realize it? For this reason:

By those very means through which one formerly perceived the Self, and by which one now regards the non-Self as "I," one seeks to know the Self—the Seer of seeing—by means of those well-known [means]. (11)
For what reason, then, does one not perceive the Self with those outward-turned cognitions that swallow up sound and the other sense-objects, as if it were a non-Self? It is said in reply:
"The eye does not see sound because it is not of the nature of that [sound];
just so, the material vision does not fully behold the Self. (12)
First, the reason for not perceiving that [Self] was stated in accordance with the inherent nature of the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception.
Now, the negation is stated in accordance with the inherent nature of the objects of cognition:
"Of the thousands of mental modifications, which possess the properties of rejection and acquisition..."
One never perceives the Self as "I," for the Self is the witness by virtue of its inwardness.
But where does this notion of discrimination reside—is it in the Self or in the non-Self? What follows from this?
If it resides in the Self, there would be a contradiction of its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), because [the Self] would then be a perceiver of the non-Self.
If, on the other hand, it resides in the non-Self, then because that too is insentient (*acaitanya*), there can be no connection with discrimination. To this it is replied:

Because of the refutation stated [in the verse]: "The state of being the fuel and the burner cannot exist in one and the same place," this distinction exists only within the intellect (buddhi), which is a differentiation based on the non-self-nature [of objects]. This [realization] does not destroy the intellect itself, just as the fruit of the plantain tree does not destroy the plantain tree.
Thus, perceiving reality in what is not reality,

having discarded all non-self entities by means of the lamp of inference, he desires through his intellect the absence of those [non-selves] by means of that [inference] which is the sole support for worldly existence. (15)

This discrimination, born of positive and negative concomitance and characterized by the distinction between the Self and the non-Self, must be understood as residing in the non-Self—like a cognition of doubt regarding a post—and not otherwise, because of the inherent nature of things, like the awakening from the perception of water in a mirage; therefore, he says:
"Established in the seed of transmigratory existence, one desires liberation through that [discrimination];
it is like a hare wishing to avoid death by closing its eyes. (16)
To strengthen this point, there is an illustration from the Śruti.
Keeping this meaning foremost, the Śruti has clearly and confidently illustrated it with the words "That which [is perceived] by the eye" and "not seen," etc. (17).
Having thus cast away everything up to the intellect, for one who investigates "Who indeed am I?", the Śruti, which transcends all means of knowledge, declares: "That thou art. (18)
Thus, the meaning of the preceding three chapters has been stated in brief.

Although this is the correct meaning of the Vedānta and is obtainable through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, it is not perceived by certain people who, despite being faithful, disregard the grace of the scriptures and the teacher because [the truth] is established by its own nature independently of anything else.
For the sake of gathering such people together, there is the citation of authorities that they themselves accept.
And the venerable teacher Bhagavatpūjyapāda has likewise cited this very point;
thus, the meaning we have explained is made perfectly clear by those who desire the welfare of all beings. (19)
Is the instruction intended for the Supreme Self (paramātman) or for the non-Supreme Self (aparamātman)? What follows from this?

If it were for the Supreme Self, the instruction would be useless, since that [Self] is liberated even without instruction. If, on the other hand, it were for the non-Supreme Self, the instruction would likewise be fruitless, because that [Self] possesses the nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) by its very own nature. Since there is thus a fault in both cases, he says: "If the Śruti speaks of both without making a distinction, then one should be like a householder."
Thus, having adopted this position and having refuted the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), [he proceeds]. || 20 ||
