And this [instruction], "That thou art," is taught by itself to one who is devoid of discrimination regarding the Self that is distinct [from the body].
This statement would be meaningful for one who knows the distinction between "you" (the object) and "I" (the subject);
for to one who lacks such knowledge, the sentence would be like singing to the deaf. (21)
And what reasoning serves as the means for that discernment of the distinction between "you" and "I"? Listen:
"For positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) apply to both the object and the word;
this very reasoning is the means of determination in the case of the thought 'I'. (22)
To explain how those two constitute reasoning, he says:
"In this state of deep sleep, the thought 'I did not see anything at all' does not negate one's own power of vision; rather, it negates the specific cognition. (23)

"When the meaning of the words has been thus understood through the authority of scripture and worldly convention, the Śruti says 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi) in order to remove the delusion of the hearer. || 24 ||
In this context, that meaning in which the word *tvam* (thou) functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is now stated:
"That very state of the word 'I' which rests in the light of the inner self is expressed as 'Thou art That'; the fruit therein is liberation. (25)
Furthermore, there is another example of positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka):
"Just as the self is not itself distinguished by the hand that has been severed and cast away, so it is not distinguished by anything else that remains. (26)
Just as all these ornaments, though they appear beautiful, are superimposed by ignorance, so too everything becomes unreal once the Self is known. (27)
Therefore, every qualification is equal to a severed hand;
thus, by virtue of being non-self, the knower is liberated from all qualifications.
The Self alone, as pure consciousness, should always be grasped while abandoning the object of knowledge;
even that which is grasped as "I" is indeed like a limb that has fallen away. || 29 ||
"Because it is an object of perception, this notion of 'I' is not a property of the Self, just like a jar or other objects;
likewise, other cognitions should be understood [in the same way], and therefore the Self is indeed stainless. || 30 ||
The summary of all principles:
"The realization of eternal liberation arises from the sentence and not from anything else;
and the realization of the meaning of the sentence is preceded by the recollection of the meanings of the individual words. (31)
Through positive and negative concomitance, the meaning of the word is certainly remembered;
in this way, one realizes the Self as being free from suffering and inactive.
From such statements as "He is with the gods," a clearer cognition arises regarding the inner self, just as it does from the statement "You are the tenth. || 33 ||
An illustration of one who has fallen into doubt:
"Just as a person, not seeing himself as the 'tenth' due to the loss of the notion of 'nine,' would desire to know his own self; so it is with [the soul]. (34)

"Because his eyes are bound by ignorance, his intellect is perpetually carried away by desires; he does not perceive the Self, which is pure consciousness and solitary, just as one fails to see the tenth man. (35)
He says how this person, whose vision is thus veiled by the film of ignorance, is awakened:
"Just as a dreamer, when awakened by some cause within the dream itself, no longer perceives the instrument, the action, or the agent as belonging to the dream, by his own nature. (36)

Likewise, this one who knows the Self, having been awakened by the correct hearing [of the scriptures], does not perceive the teacher, the scripture, or even the deluded one as other than his own self. (37)

Does he, through the sentence, understand himself as entirely secluded from the whole of saṃsāra, or not? To this we reply: because realization consists solely in the remainder of the knowledge of the unchanging [Self], it is said: "Just as the snake in the stick comes to rest in the stick, so the world undoubtedly comes to rest in the eternal realization through the sentence. (38)

Whence is this? Because, when he says "seeing" (paśyan) with such emphasis, that which is the inner self (pratyaktva)—unborn, undecaying, without prior or posterior, and infinite—is indicated by the word "thou" (tvam). || 39 ||
It is only by the higher knowledge arising from such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) that [ignorance] is sublated;
for it is determined that there is no form other than this [Self]. Because there is no apprehension of anything else, that [ignorance] is the seed of both dreams and waking states. (40)
An illustration for the sake of strengthening this point is as follows:
"The Viśva and Taijasa are considered to be bound by both cause and effect;
the Prājña is bound by the cause alone; but these two [states] do not exist in the Turya. (41)
"Dream occurs for one who perceives otherwise; sleep belongs to one who does not know reality.
When the perversion of these two is exhausted, one attains the fourth state. || 42 ||
Likewise, there is this illustration from the venerable Śaṅkarācārya:
"The ignorance called deep sleep is the seed of dreaming and waking;
it becomes utterly consumed by the awakening of the Self, just as a burnt seed ceases to sprout."
Thus has this matter been declared by our venerable teachers from Gauḍa and Draviḍa:
the Lord, who perceives "I" and so forth, has ignorance alone as His limiting adjunct (upādhi). || 44 ||

In this regard, he states that non-apprehension—which is like the apprehension of something otherwise and serves as the seed for such erroneous apprehension—is indeed a property of the non-Self (anātmadharma):
"This knowledge, I the knower, and this object of knowledge"—these three, which the changeless one perceives, are merely his darkness (tamas). (45)

Since this is so, he states by means of an illustration that the connection with its own effects—which constitute a second entity—belongs only to that very *tamas* in the form of a seed, characterized as a property of the mind (*citta*), and not to the changeless Self (*ātman*):

"Just as there is a conjunction of form and light belonging to that which is subject to modification, so too is the connection with pleasure, pain, and the like [belonging] only to the mind, which is subject to modification. (46)

Demonstrating this through both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), he says: "When the subject to modification has set, due to its state of non-modification during the [state of] perfect serenity (saṃprasāda), not even the slightest second thing touches the Self of the one who sees. (47)
This very Self is the embodiment of immutable knowledge;
just as it is in the state of deep sleep (prājña), so too is it at the two ends of dreaming and waking.
Though seeing, because of its changelessness, it does not see a second [object].
Thus, for one who possesses such knowledge, there is no reliance on the notions of "mine" and "I," just as darkness cannot exist before a person holding a brilliant lamp.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

Just as prior to awakening there is no establishment of any entity other than duality, so too, upon awakening, there is no establishment of the intellect and so forth apart from the inner self (pratyagātman). 50.
This very wise one, perceiving within himself the Self which is devoid of both rejection and appropriation, allows for everything and negates everything.
Permission would consist in the acquisition of the nature of duality; negation arises from the absence of that nature. (51)
Since everything has been stated, this is the conclusion:

"That knowledge which is established in the ultimate reality, which is determined by all the Vedāntas, and which dispels the darkness [of ignorance] in the intellect—that very thing has been declared by me. (52)
This much has been stated here:
"There is no knower of the Self other than I; there is no one more ignorant than I. He who, knowing this, truly understands it, is the highest among the knowers of Brahman. (53)
Having thus known the Self, should one engage in activity, or should one desist, or should one adopt a state of "letting go"? It is said:

Since this [Self] is non-different from the object of knowledge, and because it conforms to the nature of the knowable reality, it does not cast even a sidelong glance toward either engagement or withdrawal. (54)
How is it known that this [knowledge] is non-different from the object of knowledge? Because:
"Prior to the realization of the Self, this knowledge has external objects as its secondary focus;
once the entire cycle of transmigratory existence has been destroyed, it rests solely upon the Self, according to the Śruti. (55)

Thus, for one who has realized the reality of the ultimate truth, there is no longer a relationship of subordinate and principal, because its cause has been dispelled; so he says: "Since right knowledge, by its very nature, obstructs worldly existence, it does not destroy even cessation, just as it does not destroy active engagement. (56)
By the mere once-and-for-all arising of the Self, one blocks all worldly existence;
through the simple removal of darkness, there is no other way for the mind to be otherwise.

Since space and so forth are not connected with [specific] place, time, and so on, and since they are the effects of delusion, there exists neither non-arisen nor unburnt knowledge; therefore, ignorance exists. 58.
For one whose delusion and its effects have been consumed by the fire of right knowledge, what effect remains once that which is to be sublated has ceased forever? (59)
The resolution has been stated that because ignorance is utterly destroyed by its very nature, nothing whatsoever remains. Now follows another traditional resolution:

"Just as one does not immediately release the trembling caused by a snake even after the snake has vanished, so too the knower of the Self continues to perform the effects of delusion even though all delusion has been destroyed. (60)
Since the seed of worldly activity has been destroyed, therefore,
just as a tree whose roots have been uprooted perishes through withering alone,
so too does the body perish through the very cessation of that which is of the nature of the awakened Self. 61.
Then, in order to refute the position of the "unguished" (alepaka), he says:

"If one who perceives the non-duality of the Buddha were to act according to his own whims, what difference would there be between dogs and those who perceive reality in their consumption of impurity? (62)
Why is it not so? Because:
"From unrighteousness arises ignorance, and from that comes acting according to one's own whims.
How could that [ignorance] exist in the performance of dharma, wherein even dharma is not accepted? (63)
Refuting the notion that Hari acts according to his own whims, the All-Seeing One said: "Whose every undertaking... and "And [his actions] are manifest... (Gītā 3.20; 4.26). 64.
Let alone that knowledge which devours the seeds of all worldly activity—which is impossible even in the state of one seeking liberation—acting as one pleases is likewise impossible.
Thus it is said: "For he who is detached from something does not engage in that thing."
Since he is detached from the three worlds, why would one who desires liberation strive for this? || 65 ||
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Even when tormented by hunger, one does not desire to eat poison; knowing that thirst has been quenched by sweet food, a person who is not deluded does not long for it. (66)
Therefore, for one who has realized the supreme reality, acting according to one's own whims is not possible in the slightest, even while desiring liberation.
Attachment to the fields of mental exertion is a sign of ignorance;
how can there be lush greenery in that tree which has fire within its hollow? (67)
From what source does this realization of the Self arise, which brings about the complete fulfillment of all human goals? It is said:

Knowledge arises for one who is established in the qualities beginning with humility (amānitva) and who possesses the means beginning with non-hatred (adveṣṭṛ), but not for one whose mind is directed outward. (68)

Once the knowledge of the Self has arisen, do qualities such as humility—which consist of cessation—cease because they are effects of ignorance, just as worldly activity does, or not? We say: "No. What is the reason? Because the nature of the Supreme Self is not in conflict with the scriptures on cessation; it is not, however, by virtue of a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). How then? Listen: For one in whom the awakening to the Self has arisen, qualities such as non-enmity occur without effort, and not as something requiring formal means. (69)
Since this is so, therefore:
One who desires to take up this book should be diligent in the means such as freedom from pride; he must not be of evil conduct, for this [work] follows the innermost dharma.

This text must not be given to one who is not dispassionate toward saṃsāra, nor to one who has not cast off desires; nor should this introduction to the meaning of Vedānta be given to one who lacks devotion. 71.
Once this has been correctly understood as it has been explained, nothing further remains to be known;
yet, one would not understand this directly if karma were not first eliminated. (72)
Those ascetics who have cast aside all ritual actions, whose intellects are inclined toward the inner Self,
who are free from desire and peaceful, know this as it has been described.
Having served the pair of lotus feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara, he obtained this stainless knowledge of the state of the Paramahaṃsa, which dispels the darkness within the heart.
Let there be no contrary opinion regarding this; therefore, it should be examined by the wise and the virtuous everywhere for the sake of purity, for the virtuous are the supreme authority. (74)
Even a well-spoken word, though beautiful, does not shine for those who lack greatness, just as the stainless sun does not shine for those who see only at night;
yet it truly shines for those of pure mind, just as a vast treasury of great wealth shines for those whose thirst has been cast away.

Having properly worshipped with devotion that [knowledge] which follows the foot of Viṣṇu, which destroys all worldly existence, and which Śaṅkara imparted through yoga to the omniscient one established in Brahman who was accompanied by hosts of sages—I, having received from that treasure-house of excellent qualities this knowledge which shines like the Gaṅgā and is illuminated by Vedānta, have out of compassion spoken it for the destruction of the multitude of births and deaths for those who are suffering. (76)

Salutations to that most venerable Guru, the worshipful one, who—by means of the very probe of logic—dispelled the darkness that is the seed of our entire worldly existence and revealed the divine knowledge residing within the womb of the Vedanta; a knowledge that is radiant, stainless, the destroyer of ignorance in our minds, and which is never obstructed even regarding objects beyond the reach of the senses. (77)
This excellent statement of the connection has been illustrated for every verse;
having understood this, one will certainly be able to explain the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*. (78)
Thus ends the fourth chapter. 4.
